versions.notes: The official eleven-page article uses printed pp. 551–561, retains the version-6/7 result family, and links the author repository recorded separately with its current access status. Canonical claims use the proceedings folios; revision-only claims use article pagination.

inclusion.rationale: The paper places a differentiable attention read over a growing tape of prior recurrent states inside each LSTM update, then combines that intra-sequence read with cross-sequence attention through shallow and gated deep fusion. It supplies a recurrent intra-attention branch explicitly cited in the Transformer background, without equating its sequential memory update with recurrence-free Transformer self-attention.

significance.beginner: Instead of asking one LSTM state to summarize everything read so far, the reader keeps a tape of earlier hidden and memory vectors. Each new word softly chooses which earlier entries matter before the recurrent gates write the next state; for sentence pairs, another attention stream can consult the other sentence.
significance.expert: LSTMN scores prior hidden states with the current input and preceding adaptive summary, uses the resulting distribution to read aligned hidden and cell tapes, and substitutes those summaries into the gated recurrent update. Shallow fusion composes intra-attentive encoder and decoder modules with cross-attention; deep fusion recurrently stores the source summary through an additional gate.

limitations: Every token update remains sequential and conditions on earlier adaptive recurrent state; the architecture is not a recurrence-free all-position sequence mixer.
The work concentrates on attentive reads from the tape and leaves attention-controlled writes to future investigation.

The tape is said to grow until an upper memory-span bound, but the bound and eviction or truncation rule are not specified; table phrases such as memory size 300 refer to vector dimensionality rather than a documented slot cap.
Despite its machine-reading framing, the paper evaluates language modeling, sentiment, and natural language inference rather than a question-answering or reading-comprehension benchmark.
Its induced token relations receive only task-level supervision, remain soft and undirected, and are illustrated with selected examples rather than evaluated against structural annotations.
The language-model, sentiment, and inference studies use three bounded datasets and selected comparator families; they provide no repeated-run variance, confidence intervals, or statistical tests.
The strongest canonical SNLI system has a reported count of 3.4 million parameters, substantially more than several listed recurrent comparators, which the authors caution limits direct comparison.

ArXiv result tables change materially: version 3 reports 92.3/89.1 for deep fusion, versions 4–5 report an improved 92.1/89.0 variant, and versions 6–7 plus the proceedings omit that variant without explaining its removal.
The two LSTMN sentiment rows change from 49.3/87.3 and 49.8/87.9 through version 5 to 47.6/86.3 and 47.9/87.0 in versions 6–7 and the proceedings without an explanation.
The paper-linked SNLI-attention repository returned HTTP 404 when checked on 23 August 2026; its recorded URL therefore supplies no currently accessible immutable code revision or checkpoint.

Transformer includes Cheng in the grouped prior self-/intra-attention task citation whose first listed context is reading comprehension; that context does not establish adoption of the recurrent memory tape, its gated fusion equations, or its empirical results.

inclusion.rationale: The paper factors cross-sentence soft alignment into independent attend, compare, and aggregate computations, producing an attention-only textual-entailment system whose core avoids recurrent and convolutional encoders. Its optional feed-forward intra-sentence attention adds only bucketed relative-distance bias. The Transformer cites this recurrence-free attention case in its background, but the citation does not establish direct mechanism adoption.

significance.beginner: The model aligns each word or local phrase in one sentence with a soft blend from the other, compares every aligned pair separately, then sums those local judgments before classifying the sentence pair. The optional same-sentence pass adds a small notion of distance without requiring recurrent reading order.
significance.expert: Shared feed-forward F projections turn every cross-sentence pair into a dot score, bidirectional softmaxes form aligned phrases, shared G networks compare each pair, and H classifies the sums. The optional F_intra self-alignment concatenates a distance-biased same-sentence mixture; total work is O(ℓd² + ℓ²d), parallel over positions, and O(ℓd²) only under the paper’s ℓ < d assumption.

limitations: The vanilla model intentionally uses no word-order information; the optional variant supplies only learned relative-distance buckets and still fails selected sequence-sensitive cases.

The O(ℓd²) simplification depends on the paper’s ℓ < d assumption, illustrated by SNLI lengths below 80 and cited LSTM hidden dimensions of at least 300; the paper reports no measured latency or hardware speedup.

The printed multi-class cross-entropy expression lacks the conventional leading minus sign in both arXiv revisions and the proceedings article, while the text calls it a loss without specifying whether the displayed quantity is maximized or minimized.
ArXiv version 1 prints d_(i−j) in every denominator term of equation 7; version 2 and the proceedings correct the summation term to d_(i−k).
The 86.8 test accuracy is one half percentage point above the listed 86.3 systems, with no repeated-run variance, confidence interval, or significance test.
The nearly one-order parameter comparison applies to the 382K vanilla model versus the 3.4M Cheng comparator; the 582K intra-attention system is about 5.8 times smaller, excluding embeddings.
Training uses ten asynchronous update threads, selects the best development checkpoint across 50 million steps, and provides no seeds, immutable code, checkpoints, or run-level uncertainty.
Table 3 contains selected examples rather than an aggregate error taxonomy; all compared systems miss highlighted antonym, numerical, and sequence-sensitive cases.

Transformer cites the work as an attention-only textual-entailment case; that context does not establish adoption of its attend–compare–aggregate factorization, distance bias, SNLI training recipe, or results.
ACL states that 2016-and-later Anthology material is CC BY 4.0 while excluding third-party content; any atlas diagrams should still be redrawn and attributed.

It describes Sub-Batch Normalization, character n-gram input bags for translation, and shallower wider experiment configurations. versions.title: Neural Machine Translation in Linear Time
versions.label: Canonical arXiv version 2

bibliography.citation: N. Kalchbrenner, L. Espeholt, K. Simonyan, A. van den Oord, A. Graves, and K. Kavukcuoglu, “Neural Machine Translation in Linear Time,” arXiv:1610.10099v2, 15 March 2017.

versions.notes: The canonical nine-page revision estimates an encoder width at 1.2 times the English source length, uses layer normalization, doubles both translation stacks to 30 blocks, and reports 1.31 in a Hutter table labeled bits per byte plus 23.75/26.26 BLEU in its translation tables. Nearby prose calls the Hutter metric bits per character, and the introduction instead prints 22.85/25.53 BLEU with incompatible 0.380/0.389 bits-per-character values, so none of these differences is silently repaired.

inclusion.rationale: ByteNet replaces sequence-aligned recurrent translation computation and explicit attentional pooling with stacked masked and unmasked dilated convolutions, a resolution-preserving source representation, and variable-length dynamic unfolding. The Transformer directly cites it as a parallel convolutional predecessor with logarithmic distant-position paths, making it essential convergence context without establishing adoption of ByteNet’s equations or training recipe.

significance.beginner: Instead of squeezing a source into one vector or forming an attention-weighted source pool at every target step, ByteNet keeps a column-wise source representation and stacks a convolutional decoder above it. Masking hides future target characters, dilation lets information cross long spans in fewer layers, and unfolding continues until an end symbol.
significance.expert: The canonical revision factorizes p(t|s) autoregressively; stacks a masked, dilated CNN decoder over an unmasked dilated CNN encoder; estimates an extended source representation at 1.2|s| for English–German; uses residual ReLU or multiplicative blocks with layer normalization; and reports analytic c|S|+c|T| work with c≈log d and short convolutional paths.

limitations: The work is represented as an arXiv preprint family. The arXiv and Google Research records identify no peer-reviewed conference or journal publication for this title.
Position-wise decoder computation can run in parallel during training, but ordinary target generation remains autoregressive and sequential across output positions.

For a fixed receptive field, the stated convolutional work is linear in sequence length. If the dependency field must scale with sequence length, c≈log n makes the corresponding work O(n log n). Table 1 is an architectural analysis, not matched wall-clock, throughput, memory, or accelerator evidence.

Version 2’s dynamic-unfolding experiment fixes the English–German representation bound to 1.2|s|. It reports no sensitivity study for that bound or evidence that the same ratio transfers to other language directions.

The translation comparisons mix phrase, word, word-piece, BPE, and character systems with different data, architectures, decoding methods, and ensemble conditions. They are not a controlled isolation of convolution, dilation, or unfolding.

Canonical version 2 is internally inconsistent: the introduction reports 22.85/25.53 BLEU with 0.380/0.389 bits per character, while Tables 2 and 4 report 23.75/26.26 with 0.521/0.532. The source supplies no reconciliation.

The Hutter table caption says bits per byte while the result prose says bits per character; the atlas retains the source’s terminology rather than asserting that the units were independently reconciled.

Version 2 still reports a 315-character language-model receptive field after changing the number of repeated dilation cycles. That value is retained as a reported result, not presented as independently re-derived from the schedule.

The first and second revisions describe materially different architecture sizes, normalization, input features, optimization, decoding, and results. Their changes do not form controlled ablations and values must not migrate across versions.
The gradient-magnitude heatmaps are selected sensitivity visualizations, not supervised word alignments, an attention mechanism, a causal attribution method, or a quantitative alignment evaluation.

The paper reports no random seeds, repeated-run dispersion, confidence intervals, significance tests, immutable code or checkpoint, complete data manifest, exact BLEU implementation, or measured training and decoding speed.

The Transformer cites ByteNet’s convolutional parallelism, logarithmic distant-position path, and 23.75 BLEU result as comparison context; it does not state that Transformer components derive from ByteNet’s mask, dilation schedule, dynamic unfolding, model dimensions, or experiments.

ArXiv’s non-exclusive distribution license authorizes arXiv to distribute the submission; it does not grant third parties a general content-reuse or repository-redistribution license. The atlas links the paper and redraws any future explanation.

uncertainties.note: Both immutable arXiv revisions were compared. The first posting contains the core convolutional sequence model, while the second materially revises unfolding, normalization, architecture, training, decoding, and results.
The authored PDFs print Aäron van den Oord and Alex Graves. The Google Research page expands Alex to Alexander; the authored version controls the work and version author lists.
Version 2 does not explain whether its introductory and tabular BLEU and bits-per-character pairs refer to different checkpoints, scoring procedures, or stale edits.

bibliography.venue: Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning

versions.notes: The canonical ten-page PMLR article uses the updated result rows also found in version 3 and explicitly identifies 41.62 as a ten-model English–French ensemble. Its four-page supplement separately supplies initialization derivations and one selected eight-layer attention example. Evidence locators use PDF leaves 1–10 rather than translating them into volume folios 1243–1252.

inclusion.rationale: The work is the immediate fully convolutional encoder–decoder predecessor that the Transformer explicitly contrasts on path length and computation, benchmarks in translation, cites for learned positional embeddings, and includes among the encoder–decoder attention mechanisms it mimics. ConvS2S is essential convergence evidence while remaining distinct from Transformer self-attention.

significance.beginner: The encoder and decoder replace recurrent state chains with stacked sliding windows. Every target layer gets its own source-attention read, learned position tags preserve order, and training can process positions together even though translation is still generated one token at a time.
significance.expert: Contiguous stride-one convolutions with GLUs and scaled residual paths yield receptive field 1 + L(k − 1); causal cropping protects the autoregressive decoder; each decoder layer applies a dot-product cross-attention hop over top encoder states plus source embeddings; and tailored initialization and variance scaling stabilize deep stacks.

limitations: “Fully convolutional” describes the encoder and decoder state computation, not non-autoregressive generation: training-time positions parallelize, while beam decoding remains left-to-right.

For fixed kernel width, the path between increasingly distant positions grows linearly with sequence length. ConvS2S does not inherit ByteNet’s dilated logarithmic path, and the large English–French decoder can use only 25 prior target words.

The translation comparisons mix word, BPE, and word-piece systems, data filtering, BLEU conventions, model sizes, decoding, and ensemble conditions. English–Romanian uses detokenized BLEU while the other translation tasks use tokenized BLEU.

The paper’s broad state-of-the-art framing is not universal: it reports a 26.03 sparse-mixture English–German single run above ConvS2S’s best single run of 25.39 and argues that the mixture resembles an ensemble.

The speed table spans different GPU generations, CPU core counts, beam widths, and BLEU levels; the paper itself says CPU rows are not directly comparable, so the reported ratios are not a matched hardware benchmark.

Position, attention-layer, depth, and kernel studies use a separate 160K-target-vocabulary English–German setup with vocabulary selection and BLEU before unknown replacement; their absolute scores do not transfer to Table 1.
The paper reports no isolated ablation for GLUs, residual paths, variance scaling, initialization, or the zⱼᵘ + eⱼ attention value construction.
The supplement interprets attention layers from one selected English–German example rather than a representative sample, gold alignment task, or quantitative structural evaluation.

The reported results average three initialization seeds, but the paper gives no dispersion, confidence interval, significance test, exact random seeds, dropout probabilities, tuned German length exponent, word-count batch cap, or precise ensemble-combination rule.

The paper links source code and pretrained models, but does not pin the experiment commit, checkpoint identities, complete data manifest, or exact evaluation commands needed to reconstruct every table.
ArXiv versions change reported results without changing the core equations. Version 3’s ambiguous “former” wording is resolved only by its table and the explicit published English–French sentence.

Transformer citations establish direct comparison, a familiar encoder–decoder attention route, and a learned-position alternative; they do not establish that ConvS2S’s convolutions, GLUs, or layerwise attention caused the core self-attention architecture.

The article footer establishes author copyright. PMLR’s current publication agreement describes CC BY 4.0 publication, but the inspected record does not archive the 2017 agreement text; figure reuse should therefore verify the applicable grant at use time.

uncertainties.note: All three immutable arXiv revisions, the canonical PMLR article, and its separate supplement were compared; mechanism text is stable while reported translation rows change.
The published paper and surviving fairseq-lua record do not identify an immutable code commit and checkpoint set for every reported configuration.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A paper-era commit manifest, checkpoint hashes, data preprocessing record, and evaluation commands would be required for exact reconstruction.

versions.title: Attention Is All You Need
versions.label: Canonical NIPS 2017 proceedings paper

bibliography.citation: A. Vaswani et al., “Attention Is All You Need,” in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30, pp. 5998–6008, 2017.
bibliography.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
bibliography.series: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems

versions.notes: The official 11-page PDF is canonical. It consistently reports 28.4 English–German and 41.0 English–French BLEU and omits the arXiv parsing section, parameter-attention appendix, and attention-visualization appendix. Technical locators use its visible article pp. 1–11, not volume folios 5998–6008.

inclusion.rationale: The work makes self-attention the principal sequence-mixing operation in both halves of an autoregressive encoder–decoder, combines it with scaled dot products, multiple learned projection heads, explicit position signals, and position-wise computation, and reports a parallelizable training path with strong translation results. It is an architectural convergence point rather than an origin claim for attention, self-attention, encoder–decoders, or autoregressive generation.

significance.beginner: Every token can build a fresh weighted view of other permitted positions instead of waiting for a recurrent state to travel step by step. Several heads make different projected views in parallel, position signals preserve order, and a causal mask keeps the decoder from seeing future target tokens.
significance.expert: Six-layer encoder and decoder stacks combine residual connections followed by layer normalization, multi-head scaled dot-product self- and cross-attention, position-wise ReLU networks, sinusoidal input positions, tied embeddings/output weights, masked autoregressive decoding, Adam warmup, label smoothing, and byte-pair or word-piece vocabularies.

limitations: The architecture removes sequence-aligned recurrence and nontrivial-width convolution from its sequence-mixing layers, not all non-attention computation: it retains embeddings, position-wise feed-forward layers, residual paths, layer normalization, and a softmax output.
Training-time token representations can be computed in parallel within a layer, but ordinary target generation remains autoregressive and therefore sequential across output positions.
Full self-attention has quadratic O(n²d) layer cost. The proposed restricted alternative for long inputs is future work rather than an evaluated remedy in this paper.

Table 1 is an asymptotic operation and path-length analysis, not empirical evidence that shorter paths alone improve learning on long dependencies; the paper reports no length-stratified translation test.

Table 2 compares systems with different data, model families, hardware, training recipes, and ensemble conditions. Its training costs are estimates from time, GPU count, and assumed sustained FLOP rates rather than matched wall-clock measurements.

The strongest translation rows use checkpoint averaging, development-tuned beam search and length penalty, and different English–German versus English–French setups. They do not isolate a single architectural component.

Table 3 reports one English–German development condition without seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several rows change dimensions or parameter counts, and the 0.9-BLEU single-head gap does not establish a universal advantage for any number of heads.

The attention visualizations are selected qualitative examples. They provide no gold syntax or coreference evaluation, representativeness protocol, human assessment, or causal test that attention weights are faithful explanations.

The constituency-parsing experiment and visualization appendix occur in the arXiv family but are absent from the canonical proceedings PDF; their claims and locators cannot be transferred into that version.

The arXiv revisions disagree on English–French BLEU and training time: version 2 has three different values or conditions, version 3 retains a body/table mismatch, and versions 5–7 print 41.8 in the abstract and table but 41.0 in Section 6.1.
The NeurIPS landing-page metadata has a stale abstract with 165 million parameters and 27.5/41.1 BLEU, while the linked canonical PDF reports 28.4/41.0; technical claims follow the PDF.
The paper links Tensor2Tensor code but identifies no immutable commit, released checkpoints, random seeds, or fully pinned data and preprocessing artifact for exact reconstruction.

The paper’s Cheng and Parikh citations establish recurrent intra-attention and attention-only textual-entailment context, respectively; they do not establish direct adoption of either predecessor’s equations, architecture, training recipe, or results.

The paper directly cites ByteNet for parallel convolutional position computation, logarithmic distant-position paths, and the 23.75 BLEU comparison row; those references do not document adoption of ByteNet’s mask, dilation schedule, stacking, dynamic unfolding, training, or results.

NeurIPS says authors retain copyright and grant the venue a non-exclusive publication license. ArXiv versions 6–7 add narrower permission to reproduce tables and figures with attribution for journalistic or scholarly works; the atlas links the sources and does not infer a general open-content license.

The paper directly cites ConvS2S for a learned-position alternative and includes it among familiar encoder–decoder attention mechanisms, while separately contrasting its linear convolutional path and benchmarking v2-era results. This supports one scoped build-on edge but not a claim that ConvS2S caused core self-attention or that its GLUs, contiguous convolutions, or layerwise hops were adopted.

uncertainties.note: All seven arXiv revisions and the separate proceedings PDF were compared. The core architecture is already present in version 1, the output projection and several clarifications arrive in version 2, and later changes chiefly affect evidence, appendices, attribution, and rights text.

The work directly names recurrent encoder–decoders, Bahdanau-style additive attention, convolutional sequence models, earlier self-attention applications, and memory networks. Those references bound its novelty but do not make every cited work a documented causal predecessor.
Versions 5–7 do not explain whether 41.8 and 41.0 refer to different English–French runs, scoring procedures, or an uncorrected text edit.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: Versioned experiment logs, an exact code/checkpoint mapping, or an author correction would be required to reconcile the two values.

uncertainties.note: No inspected primary record ties the released Tensor2Tensor repository to an immutable revision and every reported result condition.

versions.notes: The official proceedings article is canonical and uses printed pp. 2227–2237. It adds Sections 5.6–5.7 and a published Table 7 but omits the arXiv supplement; the official four-leaf attachment remains a separate companion source.

inclusion.rationale: ELMo makes every token occurrence a task-conditioned mixture of the input layer and all internal layers of a pretrained bidirectional LSTM language model, then transfers those frozen features across six supervised tasks. It is a central recurrent, feature-based bridge from static word embeddings and language-model pretraining to later contextual pretrained encoders without being a Transformer, masked language model, or causal generator.

significance.beginner: A word no longer receives one fixed dictionary vector. Two language models read the sentence in opposite directions, and a downstream task learns how much to use the character-aware input layer and each contextual LSTM layer while the pretrained language model stays frozen.
significance.expert: ELMo jointly optimizes separate forward and backward autoregressive log-likelihoods with shared token and softmax parameters, concatenates direction-specific states at every layer, and learns a softmax-normalized task mixture with a learned scale. Its recurrent feature-extraction route, optional unlabeled domain adaptation, layer and placement ablations, and version-specific results form a distinct precursor to later Transformer fine-tuning.

limitations: The bidirectional representation consumes both left and right context. It is not a causal next-token representation and would leak future input in an ordinary left-to-right generator.

The supervised stage freezes the pretrained biLM and learns feature mixtures around task-specific architectures; optional unlabeled target-domain LM adaptation occurs first and is not end-to-end supervised fine-tuning.

The six headline rows use heterogeneous 2017-era task architectures, datasets, and metrics. Most are single estimates, no unified compute control is reported, and only a subset includes repeated-run dispersion.
The abstract's ‘up to 20%’ wording conflicts with Table 1's printed 24.9% SQuAD and 21% NER relative-error reductions; exact rows are preserved instead of harmonizing the prose.
WSD and POS probes support task-specific layer differences under their evaluators, not a universal or causal claim that one layer is syntax and another is semantics.
Pretraining uses English news text. The paper does not evaluate multilingual transfer, fairness, calibration, robustness, or broad domain shift.
The OpenReview, arXiv v1, arXiv v2, and proceedings texts contain materially different result rows and supplements; values are never moved across versions without explicit evidence.

ArXiv's non-exclusive distribution license is not a general content-reuse license. ACL's CC BY 4.0 policy excludes third-party content, and future figures should be redrawn rather than copied blindly.
The official code repository is mutable and the paper does not pin a complete experiment commit, checkpoint set, random seeds, or deterministic reproduction package.

versions.notes: The official proceedings article is canonical and uses printed pp. 328–339. It preserves version 2's 4.57 Table 7 value, reversed transfer-learning sentence, and incorrect Equation 3 denominator; the corrected v3–v5 forms remain explicitly bound to those later arXiv revisions.

inclusion.rationale: ULMFiT turns a general-domain autoregressive language model into a reusable text classifier through target-domain LM adaptation, discriminative layerwise learning rates, a slanted triangular schedule, gradual unfreezing, and long-document pooling. It is an essential whole-model fine-tuning branch between recurrent language-model transfer and later pretrained Transformer encoders, despite evaluating only English text classification.

significance.beginner: The same model first learns general language, then reads unlabeled text from the target domain, and only then learns labels. Lower layers update more cautiously and layers are unfrozen from the classifier downward so the model can adapt without discarding all pretrained behavior at once.
significance.expert: ULMFiT adapts a three-layer AWD-LSTM on WikiText-103 and target text, then applies layerwise rates divided by 2.6, corrected slanted-triangular scheduling, gradual unfreezing, concat pooling, and BPT3C. Its test ensemble, unidirectional validation ablations, low-shot data accounting, and v2–v5 corrections must remain separate.

limitations: The empirical scope is six English sentiment, topic, and question-classification datasets. The paper does not test sequence labeling, entailment, question answering, multilingual transfer, generation, or every NLP task.

Main test rows use separately trained forward and backward classifiers whose predictions are averaged; Section 5 validation ablations use unidirectional language models. This is not one bidirectional recurrent encoder.

No seeds, repeated-run dispersion, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported beyond the explicit statement that the TREC improvement is not statistically significant on its 500-example test set.

The 100-label comparisons also use target-domain unlabeled text in the semi-supervised setting: 50,000 IMDb or 100,000 AG examples. Figure 3 supplies curves rather than exact points, error bars, or raw data.

Table 5 changes dropout and classifier training duration, Table 6 adds STLR only after discriminative rates, and Table 7 is neither factorial nor parameter matched. These rows do not isolate every mechanism independently.
Figure 4 uses rising validation error as a proxy for catastrophic forgetting; it does not directly measure retained pretrained knowledge or prove that the proposed methods prevent forgetting.
Hyperparameters are tuned on IMDb, epoch counts vary by task, and the paper lacks an immutable experiment release, checkpoint hashes, complete data manifest, and exact reproduction environment.
Version 1 is a materially different FitLaM paper. Versions 3–5 correct Table 7, transfer-learning wording, and the STLR denominator, while the canonical ACL article preserves all three older forms.

The abstract's 18–24% claim applies literally to only three of six printed main result rows. The atlas uses exact dataset rows and does not promote the paper's universal-task wording beyond its evaluated scope.
ArXiv's distribution license is not a general reuse license. ACL's CC BY 4.0 policy excludes third-party content, and the Apache-2.0 code license is not assumed to cover pretrained weights.

uncertainties.note: The January 2018 FitLaM manuscript is the earliest bound public artifact and controls timeline order, while the July 2018 ACL article controls canonical bibliography.
The corrected version-5 STLR denominator and version-3 Table 7 value are preserved without silently rewriting the canonical ACL text.
The paper's code and model links do not identify one immutable experiment release, and the exposed pretrained-file directory supplies neither weight licenses nor checksums.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: An author-pinned release with checkpoints, hashes, licenses, data manifests, and evaluation commands would be required for exact reconstruction and reuse claims.

works.displayCitation: A. Radford, K. Narasimhan, T. Salimans, and I. Sutskever, “Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training,” OpenAI preprint, 11 June 2018.

versions.title: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training
versions.label: OpenAI preprint

bibliography.citation: A. Radford, K. Narasimhan, T. Salimans, and I. Sutskever, “Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training,” OpenAI preprint, 11 June 2018.

versions.notes: The official twelve-page PDF calls itself “Preprint. Work in progress.” but prints no date, report number, DOI, arXiv identifier, venue, or revision number. The official OpenAI project page supplies the 11 June 2018 release date. The paper does not call the model GPT or GPT-1. PDF creation metadata and later CDN storage headers are not promoted as publication or revision events.

inclusion.rationale: The work turns a causal Transformer language model trained on contiguous unlabeled books into one shared starting point for twelve supervised language-understanding benchmarks. Full-model fine-tuning, task-aware input serialization, and explicit comparisons with Transformer, ULMFiT, and ELMo make it a high-confidence bridge from contextual language-model transfer to general pretrained Transformer systems.

significance.beginner: One Transformer first learns by predicting the next token in books. Each labeled task is then written as one token sequence, and the same pretrained network is updated with a small task output layer plus learned boundary and delimiter-token embeddings added.
significance.expert: A twelve-layer causal Transformer maximizes an autoregressive likelihood over BooksCorpus, then all pretrained parameters are optimized for each supervised task under a task serialization and, usually, a weighted auxiliary language-model objective. The paper reports results across twelve benchmark datasets, transfer-depth and architecture ablations, and bounded zero-shot likelihood probes.

limitations: The pretraining and evaluation scope is English: BooksCorpus and twelve classification, entailment, similarity, question-answering, and story-completion benchmarks. The paper does not establish multilingual transfer or open-ended generation quality.

The paper evaluates one twelve-layer Transformer scale and one single-layer LSTM comparison; it does not provide a parameter-matched scaling study or establish a general Transformer-versus-recurrence law.
Reported benchmark values are single-system point estimates without seeds, repeated-run dispersion, confidence intervals, or significance tests.
The paper reports a token perplexity of 18.4 “on this corpus” without identifying a held-out split, evaluation protocol, or uncertainty interval.
The introduction says the GLUE improvement is 5.5 points, while Table 4 prints 72.8 versus 68.9, a 3.9-point difference. The atlas preserves the table values and flags the conflict.

The system leads the strongest displayed comparator on nine of twelve promoted dataset metrics, but trails on RTE, SST-2, and MRPC; broad state-of-the-art language is not generalized beyond those rows.
Table 5 is not a factorial or parameter-matched ablation. Removing the auxiliary objective raises the unweighted average from 74.7 to 75.0 and has mixed per-task effects.

The zero-shot probes use four task-specific likelihood heuristics and normalized curves rather than one shared prompting method, exact tabular scores, raw predictions, or supervised-equivalent evaluation.

The official release-day repository implements ROCStories only. Its README reports nondeterministic GPU behavior and a median 85.8 over ten runs versus the paper's single-run 86.5; it is not evidence that all twelve paper results were reproduced.
The paper is labeled work in progress and exposes no archival identifier or revision trail. Repository commits and later CDN metadata are not silently treated as paper versions.
The repository's MIT license covers the code tree; it is not assumed to license BooksCorpus, benchmark datasets, pretrained parameters, or the paper text.

uncertainties.note: The official project-page date, 11 June 2018, controls chronology because the paper PDF itself is undated.
“GPT” and “GPT-1” are later conventional labels absent from the inspected paper; the corpus uses the paper's title and a Radford-2018 identifier.
No official paper-version history was found, so later PDF replacement or silent textual revision cannot be reconstructed from the current CDN object alone.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: An author-maintained revision log or independently timestamped official paper copies would be needed to establish paper-version chronology.

bibliography.venue: Proceedings of the 2019 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies, Volume 1 (Long and Short Papers)

versions.notes: The official 16-page proceedings article is canonical and uses printed pp. 4171–4186. Its method and promoted result tables align with arXiv v2, while the proceedings bibliography, folios, DOI, award, and publication metadata remain version-specific.

inclusion.rationale: BERT combines a Transformer encoder with masked-token and sentence-pair pretraining so every layer can condition on both input directions, then transfers the same pretrained parameters through small task heads and supervised full-model fine-tuning. Its architecture, objectives, packed input format, broad task evidence, and explicit contrasts with Transformer, GPT, and ELMo make it a central convergence point rather than an origin claim for self-attention, contextual representation, or language-model transfer.

significance.beginner: BERT hides selected pieces of text, lets every remaining token exchange information in both directions, and learns to recover the hidden pieces while also judging whether two spans came next to each other. The resulting reader can be adapted to classification, tagging, and question answering by changing a small output head and updating the shared reader.
significance.expert: BERT pretrains a post-layer-normalized Transformer encoder with unrestricted multi-head self-attention, learned token/segment/absolute-position sums, 15%-selected masked-token cross entropy with an 80/10/10 replacement channel, and a balanced next-sentence classifier over [CLS]. BERTBase and BERTLarge are transferred by end-to-end supervised fine-tuning; versioned task tables and ablations bound claims about directionality, NSP, scale, masking, and feature extraction.

limitations: The masked-token objective predicts only selected input positions under bidirectional context. It is neither a left-to-right sequence likelihood nor evidence that the encoder alone is an autoregressive text generator.

The 80/10/10 replacement channel mitigates but does not remove the pretraining-to-fine-tuning mismatch created by [MASK], and only 15% of WordPiece positions contribute direct token targets in each sequence.

NSP uses a balanced actual-next versus random-corpus-sentence construction. The paper's task ablation supports effects under that construction and training recipe, not a universal requirement for every later encoder or sentence-pair task.

The headline task results span heterogeneous datasets, metrics, extra-data conditions, model selection, and ensembles. GLUE excludes WNLI from its displayed average, SQuAD v1.1 headline results use TriviaQA and seven systems, and comparator rows are not matched experiments.

The paper reports no confidence intervals or significance tests. Table 6 and Table 7 average five fine-tuning restarts without dispersion, BERTLarge GLUE uses development-selected restarts on small tasks, and many other rows do not report repeat counts.

The pretraining-task ablation changes objective, attention direction, target density, and fine-tuning mask together; it is not a compute-matched isolation of bidirectionality. Model-size rows also change layers, width, heads, parameters, and masked-token perplexity together.

The pretraining corpora are English BooksCorpus and English Wikipedia. The paper supplies no immutable corpus snapshots, document manifest, deduplication audit, corpus-rights analysis, multilingual evaluation, fairness audit, calibration study, or broad domain-robustness evaluation.

The appendix describes 1,000,000 steps, batch size 256, approximately 40 epochs over a 3.3-billion-word corpus, and a 90% length-128/10% length-512 schedule, while another calculation labels every batch as 128,000 words. WordPiece-token and word units and exact epoch accounting are not reconciled.
ArXiv v1, arXiv v2, and the proceedings article are not interchangeable. Headline values, GLUE rows, SQuAD 2.0, NER placement, training details, and appendix scope change across the family.

The pinned official implementation supplies Apache-2.0 code, checkpoints, and selected fine-tuning scripts, but it does not bind every reported table to immutable data snapshots, preprocessing manifests, seeds, checkpoint hashes, and a deterministic environment. Its initial README says most paper BERTLarge results do not fit 12–16 GB GPUs and labels one SQuADLarge recipe as slightly different from the paper.

ArXiv's non-exclusive distribution license is not a general reuse license. ACL's CC BY 4.0 policy applies to the proceedings article subject to third-party-material exclusions and is not extended to the arXiv manuscripts, datasets, code, or pretrained assets.

uncertainties.note: The arXiv submission history establishes 11 October 2018 as the earliest verified public artifact, so the work ID and ordering year follow version 1 rather than the 2019 proceedings date.

Both arXiv revisions and the complete proceedings PDF were compared page-aware. Canonical technical and result claims use printed NAACL pp. 4171–4186; revision-specific differences remain bound to their own unnumbered PDFs.
The paper's word, WordPiece-token, sequence-length, and epoch descriptions do not provide one fully reconciled pretraining-accounting calculation.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: Version-pinned training logs and preprocessing manifests would be required to reconcile the units and effective corpus passes.

bibliography.citation: Z. Dai, Z. Yang, Y. Yang, J. Carbonell, Q. V. Le, and R. Salakhutdinov, “Transformer-XL: Attentive Language Models Beyond a Fixed-Length Context,” in Proceedings of the 57th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, pp. 2978–2988, July 2019.
bibliography.venue: Proceedings of the 57th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics

versions.notes: The authoritative 11-page proceedings article uses printed pp. 2978–2988. Its official nine-leaf supplement supplies Appendices A–E; together they preserve the v3 technical content while remaining a separately recorded publication artifact.

inclusion.rationale: Transformer-XL directly extends the Transformer language-model substrate with cross-segment hidden-state reuse and a relative-position attention score that makes reused states positionally coherent. Its architectural derivation, controlled recurrence and position ablations, thresholded effective-context analysis, benchmark results, and explicit Transformer ancestry make it the necessary memory branch before XLNet, without assigning it the mechanisms of gated recurrent cells or external-memory networks.

significance.beginner: A Transformer usually reads a bounded window. Transformer-XL carries hidden representations from an earlier window into the next one, then describes positions by distance so an old token does not masquerade as a new token with the same absolute position number.
significance.expert: Transformer-XL stop-gradient caches the preceding segment's layerwise activations, lets current queries attend over concatenated cached and current keys/values, and replaces reused absolute positions with a four-term relative score using sinusoidal offsets, distinct content/position projections, and global biases. Its ablations separate recurrence, positional formulation, loss window, and memory budget; RECL and per-token evaluation timing remain metric- and baseline-specific.

limitations: The recurrent state is a finite cache of hidden activations, not an LSTM cell, a learned external memory, full backpropagation through prior segments, or unlimited context. Gradients stop at the cached segment boundary.
The stated O(NL) reachable path is an architectural upper bound across N layers and segment length L. It does not show that the model learns, preserves, or uses every dependency in that range.

The relative-position projection is made linear in sequence length through the relative-shift procedure, but dense attention still scores query-by-context pairs. This is not a linear-attention architecture.

Reported benchmark comparisons mix model size, data processing, training procedures, and comparator sources. The paper supplies no confidence intervals, significance tests, repeat counts, or complete table-level reconstruction package.

The Penn Treebank value 54.52 uses variational dropout and weight averaging and is scoped to results without two-step fine-tuning; the same table contains a lower 54.44 comparator that uses that additional procedure.
The One Billion Word sentence-shuffling ablation weakens cross-sentence order but does not remove every structured or long within-sentence dependency.

RECL is a model-group-relative, thresholded evaluation measure. The reported 80% and 450% comparisons use different model groups and denominators; neither is a literal memory capacity or average dependency length.

The evaluation-speed ratios compare one reported implementation with the Al-Rfou-style evaluator as per-token time on one unspecified GPU. They do not establish training speed or performance against modern cached implementations.

The generated-text evidence appears only in arXiv v3 and the ACL main-plus-supplement pair. Three top-40 samples, no human evaluation, and acknowledged hallucinations do not establish representative long-form quality.

The pinned repository contains TensorFlow and PyTorch implementations, dataset scripts, and selected training recipes, but it omits exact paper seeds, locked environments, dataset hashes, checkpoint hashes, RECL and timing programs, and a complete table reconstruction manifest.

The repository's Apache-2.0 license covers its code tree; it is not extended here to third-party datasets, cached vocabularies, downloaded checkpoints, or paper text. Each versioned arXiv record exposes CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for its corresponding manuscript, while ACL's CC BY 4.0 policy applies only to the proceedings article subject to third-party-material exclusions.

uncertainties.note: The arXiv record establishes 9 January 2019 as the earliest verified public artifact. A repository README label suggesting a 2018 preprint is not used as publication chronology.
Complete versioned PDFs and sources establish that v1 has seven authors and v2 onward has six; the work-level author list follows the canonical ACL paper without projecting it backward.
No inspected primary source explains William W. Cohen's removal between arXiv v1 and v2.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A version-bound author or repository record explaining the change would resolve the reason without altering the observed metadata.

works.title: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners
works.displayCitation: A. Radford, J. Wu, R. Child, D. Luan, D. Amodei, and I. Sutskever, “Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners,” OpenAI technical report (2019; publicly announced 14 February 2019).

date.note: The report itself is undated; the official project page supplies the public date.

dateEvidence.locator: OpenAI project page dated 14 February 2019 and linking the technical report

versions.title: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners
versions.label: OpenAI technical report

bibliography.citation: A. Radford, J. Wu, R. Child, D. Luan, D. Amodei, and I. Sutskever, “Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners,” OpenAI technical report, 2019.

versions.notes: The official 24-leaf report prints no date, report number, venue, DOI, arXiv identifier, revision label, folios, or reuse license. The dated OpenAI page establishes public availability; no official revision ledger was identified. Later checkpoint releases and the separate Release Strategies report are not versions of this artifact.

inclusion.rationale: The report scales the GPT-style causal Transformer and evaluates whether task descriptions, examples, and textual formats can elicit multiple downstream behaviors without changing model parameters. Its byte-level subword pipeline, WebText construction, four-size analysis, prompt-dependent successes and failures, overlap audit, and direct continuity with GPT make it a central generative-transfer branch, while the evidence does not support origin claims for language modeling, Transformers, prompting, or scaling.

significance.beginner: GPT-2 asks whether one next-token model trained on broad web text can be steered into several tasks by writing the task as text, sometimes with examples, without retraining the model. Larger models often improve, but translation, question answering, and summarization expose how far the behavior remains from a reliable general-purpose system.
significance.expert: The report combines a 1,024-token pre-layer-normalized causal Transformer, 50,257-symbol byte-level BPE, a Reddit-link-selected 40 GB WebText corpus, and four report-era configurations up to 1,542 million stated parameters. Zero-shot denotes no task-specific parameter or architecture updates, while prompts, demonstrations, decoding rules, detokenizers, overlap, and source-specific parameter labels remain explicit experimental conditions.

limitations: The report's zero-shot label means no task-specific parameter or architecture updates. Translation and Natural Questions receive example pairs, and other tasks use special strings, candidate restrictions, scoring rules, filters, or decoding procedures; it is not consistently zero-demonstration evaluation.

The report labels its configurations 117M, 345M, 762M, and 1542M and reserves GPT-2 for the largest. Later official checkpoint documentation corrects the family to 124M, 355M, 774M, and 1558M. Both source-specific vocabularies are preserved rather than silently normalized.

The report and small-checkpoint inference code appeared together on 14 February under the contemporaneous 117M label. The medium checkpoint followed in May under 345M; August documentation corrected those public sizes to 124M and 355M while releasing 774M; November released the rounded 1.5B model under repository label 1558M. These model releases do not create technical-report revisions, and the companion Release Strategies and the Social Impacts of Language Models has its own arXiv history.

The report's displayed autoregressive objective uses product index i while its factors remain indexed by n. The intended left-to-right chain rule is clear from the surrounding prose, but the printed notation is not silently corrected in evidence descriptions.

WebText was built from outbound Reddit links with at least three karma, not Reddit comments themselves. Forty-five million eligible links were reduced to slightly over eight million documents and 40 GB after extraction, deduplication, heuristic cleaning, date filtering, and Wikipedia removal.

Full WebText, its URL manifest, exact extracted texts, deduplication rules, split, and rights manifest were not released. Link selection does not grant a license over third-party pages, and the May real-text artifact is not a reconstructible training corpus.

The report says non-English pages were deliberately filtered. A later August model card says a subreddit blocklist also excluded sexually explicit or otherwise offensive sources, but the list and operational rules were not released and that documentation must not be backdated into the February report.

Benchmark comparisons combine imported baselines, differing tokenization and detokenization, candidate restrictions, demonstrations, task hints, decoding strategies, contamination risk, and metrics. The report supplies no confidence intervals, significance tests, repeated-run dispersion, or complete prediction files.

Greater model size does not improve every printed metric monotonically: summarization weakens at the largest step and CBT common-noun accuracy falls slightly from the 762M to 1542M report configuration. Figures 1 and 4 are not compute-matched scaling laws.

The LAMBADA 63.24 accuracy uses a stop-word filter as an approximation to the requirement that the prediction end the sentence; CoQA 55 F1 includes WebText-overlapping documents; translation and Natural Questions remain far below the cited task systems; and the best-confidence Natural Questions slice must not replace 4.1% overall exact match.

The 8-gram Bloom-filter audit is normalization- and phrase-length-specific. Low measured overlap cannot rule out shorter, fuzzy, semantic, or paraphrastic memorization, and no released match list supports an independent reconstruction.

Open-ended samples include acknowledged repetition, topic drift, factual errors, memorized common passages, and explicit hand selection. The unicorn example is one selected output among ten, not representative evidence of human-level writing.

The official repository enables inference and sampling from eventually released checkpoints but omits WebText training code, optimizer and schedule details, per-model learning rates, update counts, training tokens, compute, seeds, benchmark evaluators, overlap filters, and a locked environment.

The release-day repository snapshot contains no license. A software license was added later and a January 2020 file is titled Modified MIT License; neither is extended here to the report, WebText, third-party excerpts, or a standalone weight license.

uncertainties.note: The official project page establishes 14 February 2019 as the public date; the undated PDF's ICML-template metadata is not treated as a publication claim.
The report PDF and alternate official CDN path were byte-identical when checked, and no official report revision ledger was identified. Model and companion-report releases remain separate artifacts.

The six-month page contains an internally inconsistent January/April timeline. The dated February page, repository commits, companion report, and the same six-month page's lead support February/May instead.
No exact immutable WebText snapshot, training run, or table-level evaluation package was identified.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A complete official release binding data, preprocessing, training code, seeds, checkpoints, prompts, evaluation programs, and predictions would be required for exact reconstruction.

inclusion.rationale: ORQA joins inverse-cloze initialization, dense dual-encoder retrieval, a fixed passage index, and weakly supervised marginalization over answer-bearing block–span derivations. REALM explicitly retains that framework as a comparison and fine-tuning substrate while changing the pretraining and index-update regime.

significance.beginner: ORQA learns where to look and what span to read from question–answer pairs alone. An inverse-cloze warm-up teaches semantic passage matching, then a trainable question encoder changes which fixed indexed blocks reach a jointly trained reader.
significance.expert: ORQA combines 128-dimensional BERT dual encoders, in-batch inverse-cloze pretraining, a frozen block index, a top-five block–span marginal, and an early top-5,000 retriever marginal. Its claims remain bounded by answer-string supervision, an undefined P′ in the printed loss, mixed dataset behavior, and a delayed release that covers only part of the paper evaluation surface.

limitations: The evidence is English factoid open QA over fixed Wikipedia snapshots; it does not establish generative answering, multilingual transfer, temporal updating, calibration, safety, or citation faithfulness.
The evidence block encoder and precomputed index remain fixed during QA fine-tuning, so end-to-end refers to the trainable question encoder and reader rather than full index learning or refresh.
Answer-string matching can admit spurious derivations, examples with no retrieved match are discarded, and dataset construction and lexical biases differ substantially across the five evaluations.
BM25 remains stronger on reported TriviaQA and SQuAD tests, and the paper notes that 128-dimensional dense vectors can lose rare exact lexical distinctions.
Tables and figures report single values without repeated-seed variance, confidence intervals, significance tests, or an immutable experiment manifest.

The corrected public release limits fine-tuning/modeling support to Natural Questions and WebQuestions rather than all paper datasets while retaining CuratedTREC preprocessing and evaluation; paper, code, GCS objects, Wikipedia, and benchmarks retain separate provenance and rights.

uncertainties.note: Every inspected paper version writes P′ in the full-loss marginal although only P is defined; later code is consistent with P, but no author erratum was found.

inclusion.rationale: XLNet is a convergence node: it trains over sampled factorization orders, uses target-aware query and content streams to avoid revealing a target token, and explicitly incorporates Transformer-XL recurrence and relative positions while addressing limitations the authors attribute to BERT-style masked pretraining. Its controlled comparisons and component ablations are historically important, but objective, backbone, data, compute, and optimization must remain separately attributed.

significance.beginner: XLNet changes the order in which positions are predicted, not the written order of the sentence. Across sampled prediction orders, a word can use context from both sides; a query stream marks where to predict without exposing the answer, while Transformer-XL memory carries bounded prior context.
significance.expert: XLNet optimizes a sampled permutation-language-model objective with partial, span-based target selection; implements target-aware content and query attention; and inherits detached segment recurrence, relative positions, and relative segment scores. Its evidence must preserve the best-of-three BERT comparison, five-run ablations, version-specific recipes, and paper/code input-format conflict.

limitations: The input token sequence remains in natural order; only factorization and attention visibility are permuted. Describing shuffled input words would be incorrect.
Equation 3 is an expectation over factorization orders, while training samples orders and predicts only a partial set of positions; it does not enumerate every permutation or every target term.

Two-stream attention is a pretraining device for targets whose identities must be hidden. The downstream model uses the content stream; the query stream is not a universal two-copy inference architecture.
Transformer-XL memory is finite and detached. It extends reachable context but does not provide unlimited recall or backpropagation through all prior segments.
The controlled WikiBooks comparison uses a best-of-three BERT envelope and says hyperparameters are the same in the caption but almost identical in prose. It is not one matched run with uncertainty.

Table 6 gives medians over five runs without dispersion or significance tests. Several rows alter multiple components, and adding NSP improves RACE slightly while worsening the other printed columns; only a mixed result is supported.

The scaled system combines a permutation objective, Transformer-XL backbone, more and different data, larger batches, longer training, optimization changes, and task-specific procedures. Headline gains cannot be assigned to the objective alone.
v1, the NeurIPS article and supplement, and arXiv v2 are materially different artifacts. Later rows and corrections are not silently moved into the canonical proceedings version.
The canonical prose places CLS first, while the pinned implementation places it last and left-pads, agreeing with v1. The actual paper-run packing order remains unresolved.

The official code is Apache-2.0, but that license does not cover the paper, training corpora, or externally hosted checkpoints. The two README checkpoint links returned 404 when checked, and the released Base model was explicitly not the paper Base model.

Exact corpus snapshots, preprocessing outputs, seeds, full evaluation programs, immutable model hashes, and a complete rights manifest were not identified; most headline tables omit repeat counts and uncertainty.

uncertainties.note: The arXiv record contains exactly two revisions, and the separate NeurIPS main article plus supplement define the canonical artifact boundary.
Canonical prose and pinned code conflict on CLS placement and padding.

versions.notes: The arXiv ledger contains exactly one submission. Its 13-leaf PDF has no stable printed folios, so claims use structural section, table, appendix, and footnote anchors. No official proceedings or journal version was identified in the inspected primary indexes; that is an audit result rather than proof of universal absence.

inclusion.rationale: RoBERTa is a central controlled-recipe study rather than a new encoder architecture or pretraining objective. It retains BERT's Transformer encoder, masked-token training, and full-model adaptation while testing masking refresh, sequence packing and NSP, batch scale, byte-level BPE, data, and duration; the resulting evidence changed how nominally comparable pretrained models were interpreted.

significance.beginner: RoBERTa keeps the recognizable BERT reader but asks what happens when its training recipe is repaired and scaled: masks refresh, text is packed differently without next-sentence prediction, batches grow, and data and training increase. The lesson is that training choices can matter as much as a new architecture label.
significance.expert: RoBERTa separates several recipe contrasts—dynamic masking, input packing with or without NSP, compute-matched batch scaling, and byte-level BPE—before accumulating data and duration changes. Its tables require careful treatment of confounds, nonmonotonic rows, medians, historical ensembles, task-specific procedures, and artifact-license scope.

limitations: RoBERTa retains BERT's encoder and masked-language-model family; it is not a newly invented architecture or objective.

Dynamic masking is not uniformly better in Table 1: it improves SQuAD 2.0 F1 and SST-2 slightly but lowers MNLI-m slightly, with medians over five random initializations of unclear pretraining-versus-fine-tuning scope.

Table 2 changes both NSP and sequence construction. It does not isolate loss removal from packing, and the final FULL-SENTENCES choice crosses document boundaries and is not the numerically strongest DOC-SENTENCES row.
The compute-matched batch experiment is nonmonotonic: the 2K row is strongest on its reported metrics, while 8K is selected partly for parallelism.
The paper follows GPT-2's byte-level BPE for universal encoding despite slightly worse early results on some tasks; it does not establish an accuracy gain from that tokenizer.

The cumulative Table 4 rows change corpus quantity and diversity together, then extend training. Packing, NSP, tokenizer, length schedule, cleaning, batch, and processed examples also differ from the imported BERT row, so no single switch explains the total gain.
The stated 1,024-V100 one-day estimate applies to a 100K-step BooksCorpus plus Wikipedia run, not necessarily the full 500K-step, 160GB training run.

GLUE test results use 5–7-model ensembles and task-specific procedures, while development values are medians over five runs. SQuAD and RACE have different single-model and external-data conditions; results are not interchangeable.

The five corpora are English and lack a single immutable snapshot or umbrella rights manifest. Code and checkpoint licenses do not license BooksCorpus, Wikipedia, CC-News, OpenWebText pages, or Stories.

The initial fairseq code and checkpoints were released around the paper, but the paper and snapshot do not bind every table to exact corpora, filters, pretraining seeds, configs, checkpoints, evaluation commands, or hashes.

The paper uses arXiv's non-exclusive distribution license, not a general content-reuse license. The initial README applies BSD 3-Clause to fairseq software and pretrained models, while the separate patent grant defines its scope as fairseq software. A later MIT repository state is not backdated here.

uncertainties.note: The arXiv history contains exactly one version posted 26 July 2019; PDF creation metadata and README promises do not override the repository ledger.
The paper does not state whether each five-initialization median uses independent pretraining runs or only downstream fine-tuning initializations.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: Run-level configurations or author clarification would be required.

inclusion.rationale: T5 makes heterogeneous NLP tasks comparable through one text-to-text interface, then audits architectures, denoising objectives, corpus choices, transfer strategies, and scale inside that framework. Its encoder–decoder span-reconstruction recipe, launch C4 pipeline, original mixed supervised and unsupervised pretraining, and historically strong fine-tuned results form a central convergence node, while most fine distinctions among denoising variants remain modest.

significance.beginner: T5 rewrites many language tasks into the same simple shape: read text and write text. It compares how that shared reader-writer should learn from missing spans, filtered web pages, labeled tasks, and larger training budgets, so learners can separate the common interface from the recipe choices that made it work well.
significance.expert: T5 combines a pre-normalized encoder–decoder Transformer, head-specific bucketed relative-logit biases, sentinel-delimited span reconstruction, launch-time TFDS C4 1.0.0, mixed supervised and unsupervised pretraining, and task-specific fine-tuning. Its broad validation study and final historical results require version-aware C4 provenance, compute-versus-parameter controls, bundled-change cautions, and explicit paper/code/data/checkpoint rights boundaries.

limitations: The study usually varies one factor at a time and explicitly may miss interactions; the final T5 recipe bundles several choices that were not isolated factorially.
Only the baseline was trained ten times. Most variants were single runs whose significance convention borrows baseline variance rather than estimating per-variant uncertainty.
Tables 1–13 use validation data. Table 14 uses test data except SQuAD, whose largest model was evaluated on validation because the test server could not run it.
The full encoder–decoder architecture comparison is approximately compute-matched but not parameter-matched: its two stacks carry about twice the parameters of the decoder-only alternatives.
The original final checkpoints use supervised downstream examples during multi-task pretraining and then task-specific fine-tuning; they are neither zero-shot systems nor C4-only checkpoints.
The final one-trillion-token T5-Base comparison bundles objective, mixture, and adaptation changes, so its gain over baseline-1T cannot be assigned to span reconstruction alone.
The 18-of-24 state-of-the-art statement and comparator rows are frozen to 24 October 2019. Translation remains below the displayed prior bests, and later leaderboards are outside the claim.
No final-training FLOP total, exact TPU slice size, wall time, energy estimate, repeated-seed final score distribution, or complete run-level reconstruction package is reported.
JMLR and arXiv v3 reverse the implemented three-sentence and five-word C4 thresholds and omit two implemented filters; arXiv v4 corrects the prose without changing the model or results.

Table 10 duplicates one adapter aggregate row that conflicts with Appendix E, and Table 13's four-model-ensemble EnRo value conflicts with Appendix E. The primary sources do not resolve either number.

Launch T5 pins TFDS C4 1.0.0. Later C4 releases changed deduplication, filtering, and splits, so the current TFDS default and catalog sizes are not byte-identical proxies for the original training corpus.

No immutable prepared C4 1.0.0 output or final-output digest was identified. The launch release supplies a reconstruction pipeline; a separately pinned 2022 official manifest covers raw crawl inputs but is not launch evidence, while transitive dependencies and grouping behavior limit bitwise reproducibility.

C4 contains third-party web text with heterogeneous rights. Apache 2.0 covers the inspected T5 and TFDS code, not the incorporated web pages; the original external GCS checkpoints have no separately identified license manifest.

A later empirical C4 audit found benchmark-text matches and demographic effects from the blocklist. Exact matching does not by itself measure performance inflation, and the audit does not reconstruct the original checkpoint training bytes.
Later T5.1.1 checkpoints change activation, dropout, weight tying, training mixture, and shapes. Those properties are not back-projected onto the original T5 family.

Source comparison confines arXiv v4's substantive text correction to C4-cleaning prose; canonical model, objective, training, and result claims remain anchored to JMLR.

It adds RoBERTaShare to XSum, reduces the headline gain to about 3.5 ROUGE, adds human evaluation, and explicitly frames unsupported hallucination as the main qualitative limitation after the arXiv version had already shown the example; it also expands release and related-work detail without changing BART's reported system scores.

inclusion.rationale: BART is a convergence node between bidirectional masked representation learning and left-to-right sequence generation. Its controlled corruption comparison, reusable encoder–decoder adaptation routes, strong historical generation results, explicit hallucination evidence, and later use as RAG's generator make it central to the path from pretrained Transformers to retrieval-augmented language models.

significance.beginner: BART learns by repairing damaged text: it can read the entire corrupted input, then write the original text one token at a time. The same pretrained model can become a classifier, tagger, summarizer, dialogue model, or translation component, while its fluent but unsupported summaries show why generation quality and factual grounding are different problems.
significance.expert: BART composes a bidirectional Transformer encoder with an autoregressive cross-attentive decoder under full-sequence denoising. Its controlled base-scale objective matrix, large infilling-plus-sentence-permutation recipe, task-specific adapters, versioned XSum comparator boundary, paper-versus-fairseq decoding conflict, and explicit BART→RAG reuse require separate treatment of causal evidence, reproduction recipes, artifacts, and rights.

limitations: The controlled objective study changes architecture and adaptation format across some replicated objective families, tunes learning rate and layer normalization separately, simplifies predecessors, and omits XLNet relative positions and recurrence; it is not a complete isolated factorial study.

Objective rankings are task-dependent: the pure language model has the best ELI5 perplexity, deletion improves all four generation perplexities over token masking, and infilling plus sentence shuffling is uniquely best on CNN/DailyMail while tying infilling for best SQuAD F1.

Large-model results compare complete systems trained under differing resources, data, preprocessing, decoding, and evidence access; they do not isolate the denoising objective as the cause of every gain.

The paper reports no pretraining optimizer, learning-rate schedule, warmup, weight decay, actual sequence length, hardware, wall time, seeds, run counts, error bars, or corruption rates for the controlled BART rows.
The human evaluation reports preference percentages and significance but not sample size, rater agreement, or the statistical test; human references beat BART 67% to 33%.
BART can hallucinate fluent information unsupported by its source; the paper's selected Science-publication example is qualitative evidence rather than an incidence estimate.

Romanian-to-English transfer is weak and prone to overfitting without back-translation, and the displayed 37.96 versus 36.80 arithmetic is +1.16 even though the prose reports the gain as +1.1; the unrounded values behind that discrepancy are not disclosed.
The paper states beam five for generation, while the official task recipe uses beam four for CNN/DailyMail and beam six for XSum; the repository recipe is not silently treated as the exact paper run.

The initial code release describes itself as needing cleanup and reproducibility work. No immutable experiment manifest binds the paper runs, complete environment, training corpus bytes, checkpoints, and human-evaluation records.

ACL article rights, arXiv distribution terms, fairseq MIT terms for code and advertised pretrained models, exact checkpoint identity, training corpora, benchmark data, and third-party material remain separate provenance and license questions.

versions.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
versions.label: Sole arXiv version 1

bibliography.citation: J. Kaplan et al., “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models,” arXiv:2001.08361v1, 23 January 2020.

versions.notes: The arXiv ledger contains one posting. The immutable PDF has thirty leaves and visible folios through 30, although the record's comments field says 19 pages; the main discussion ends on p. 19 and appendices continue through p. 30. No proceedings or journal version was established in the inspected primary records.

inclusion.rationale: Kaplan et al. make model size, dataset size, and training compute separately inspectable design variables for autoregressive Transformer language models, fit their interaction across the reported experimental range, and derive a compute-allocation rule that later lineage audits can test. The node is retained as a scale-allocation bridge, not as a universal or current prescription.

significance.beginner: The paper treats model size, training text, and computation as three separate dials, then measures what happens when one becomes the bottleneck. Its main lesson is historical and conditional: under these 2020 Transformer and WebText2 experiments, larger models trained for fewer steps looked more compute-efficient, but the fitted trend was not a timeless law.
significance.expert: The study fits autoregressive cross-entropy against non-embedding parameter count N, dataset tokens D, fixed-batch compute C, and batch-adjusted minimum compute C_min; models joint N–D and N–S_min surfaces; estimates critical-batch scaling; and derives N_opt, B_crit, S_min, and one-epoch D_opt allocations. Interpretation must preserve distinct fit constants, small-data and early-training failures, seed-scale estimates, omitted context compute, internal normalization discrepancies, extrapolation breakdown, artifact absence, and the WebText2/decoder-only scope.

limitations: The promoted laws describe autoregressive cross-entropy for primarily decoder-only Transformers trained on WebText2. They are not universal laws for every architecture, tokenizer, corpus, downstream metric, capability, or later training regime.
Smooth next-token-loss changes do not establish downstream task gains or qualitative capability changes; the paper explicitly leaves that relationship open.

N excludes vocabulary and positional embeddings, and C≈6NBS omits context-dependent attention terms. The paper warns that compute scaling may be confounded when context length is at least roughly twelve times model width.

The empirical C curves initially hold batch size fixed and are not truly optimal; C_min and S_min are counterfactual adjustments based on a measured critical-batch model rather than direct runs at every optimum.

The joint N–D fit is poor for the smallest roughly 20-million-token regime, where an epoch is only forty updates. Dropout remains fixed at 10%, and regularization and data augmentation were not optimized across scale.
One-layer models and the largest incompletely converged runs are excluded from selected power-law fits; the N–S_min form also breaks down during the early training transient.

Section 4 uses roughly 0.02 loss variation as an overfitting threshold, while Figure 22 reports run-to-run variation around 0.05. The paper does not supply a run manifest that reconciles those settings or a full repeated-seed uncertainty analysis.
The learning-rate rule is a heuristic that the paper says breaks down beyond 10^10 parameters; larger learning rates for deliberately short, compute-limited runs were not tested.

The Table 6 allocation is conditional on the fitted critical-batch and loss models, treats D_opt as one epoch, minimizes non-embedding training compute, and excludes inference cost, hardware constraints, energy, and lifecycle cost. The 0.03 serial-step exponent may be consistent with zero.

The paper's own extrapolated compute and data trends contradict one another several orders beyond the measured range; it says the laws must break down at or before that region and gives highly uncertain intersection values.

No immutable official code, run manifest, released WebText2 corpus, model checkpoint, exact training-data manifest, or complete rights manifest was established. ArXiv's non-exclusive distribution license covers repository distribution of the article, not general reuse of the paper, third-party web text, code, or model artifacts.

uncertainties.note: The arXiv history contains exactly one version posted 23 January 2020; the record's 19-page comment does not replace the immutable PDF's thirty-leaf evidence envelope.
No released WebText2 payload, URL list, prepared-data digest, or item-level rights manifest was identified.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: An immutable official corpus manifest and authoritative rights documentation would be required for reconstruction and reuse claims.
