versions.notes: The canonical package is a ten-leaf main PDF plus a two-leaf supplement. Neither file exposes dependable visible folios, so structural locators control claims and volume pp. 3929–3938 remain bibliographic metadata only.

inclusion.rationale: REALM joins masked-language-model pretraining to learned retrieval over a large textual corpus and makes the retrieved passage a latent variable. It is retained as the bridge from parametric Transformer pretraining to retrieval-augmented models, with extractive, infrastructure, and artifact limits kept explicit.

significance.beginner: REALM gives a language model a searchable external memory: it retrieves passages before predicting a masked word or answering a question, and training rewards passages that make the answer more likely. The paper also shows why swapping the corpus can update some facts without erasing knowledge already stored in the network.
significance.expert: REALM optimizes a top-k approximation to a discrete latent-passage marginal with dense dual encoders, a separate knowledge encoder, salient-span masking, fresh rescoring, and asynchronously rebuilt MIPS indices. Its evidence remains bound to three extractive open-QA datasets, frozen fine-tuning document embeddings, expensive TPU indexing, and a public release that does not reproduce the original ScaNN infrastructure or fully license data and checkpoints.

limitations: The paper evaluates extractive open-domain question answering rather than open-ended generation, multilingual transfer, safety, calibration, temporal robustness, or structured and multimodal knowledge.
Top-k candidate selection is approximate and non-differentiable, document embeddings are stale between index refreshes, and the document encoder/index is frozen during reported task fine-tuning.

Reported tables contain single values without repeated-seed variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests; component ablations change coupled settings and do not establish independent additive effects.

The reported pretraining system uses 64 training TPUs plus 16 TPUs for document embedding, while the public single-machine path changes retrieval infrastructure and is explicitly not expected to reach full quality.

Corpus replacement updates selected examples but does not guarantee removal of facts retained parametrically, and the released code, checkpoints, paper, Wikipedia, and CC-News have separate provenance and rights.

uncertainties.note: The inspected release does not provide an immutable complete pretraining/retrieval-corpus manifest, run ledger, or express license for the named checkpoint and data objects.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: Immutable official manifests, archived run artifacts, and authoritative object-level terms would be required for reconstruction and reuse claims.

inclusion.rationale: DPR makes answer-supervised dense passage retrieval the explicit research object, tests in-batch and BM25 hard negatives, and separates an offline passage index from a downstream reader. RAG later names DPR as its retriever and index initialization, making the bounded substrate relationship directly inspectable.

significance.beginner: DPR learns separate question and passage vectors from answer-bearing examples, so semantic matches can be searched in a precomputed Wikipedia index before a reader examines the candidates. In-batch and BM25 hard negatives teach it which plausible-looking passages to reject.
significance.expert: DPR trains BERT-base dual encoders with a contrastive softmax, answer-derived positives, in-batch positives-as-negatives, and BM25 hard negatives; it then indexes 21,015,324 100-word passages with FAISS and feeds up to 100 results to a distinct cross-encoder reader. The evidence keeps index rebuild cost, frozen-passage joint-training ablation, answer-containment metric, version deltas, and release provenance explicit.

limitations: The evidence is English factoid extractive QA over a fixed 2018 Wikipedia snapshot; tables, infoboxes, lists, and disambiguation pages are removed, and generation, multilingual transfer, temporal updating, calibration, safety, and attribution are untested.
Retrieval accuracy means that at least one returned passage contains an answer string; it is not human relevance judgment and can count spurious matches or overlook relevant paraphrases.
In-batch and BM25 negatives are not audited for false negatives, and weak positives for three datasets can inherit BM25 and answer-string biases.
BM25 remains stronger on SQuAD and can preserve rare salient phrases that dense vectors miss; hybrid rows are not uniformly superior across tasks.
Reported tables contain single values without repeated-seed variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and copied comparator blocks were not uniformly rerun.
The paper profiles full dense-index rebuilding rather than incremental insertion, deletion, refresh correctness, or knowledge editing; its dense and BM25 throughput units are not normalized alike.

The public repository, downloadable checkpoints, embeddings, indices, Wikipedia passages, benchmark derivatives, paper, and dependencies do not share one demonstrated license or immutable experiment manifest.

uncertainties.note: The canonical paper calls the corpus units 100-word passages but later compares ORQA using the phrase 100 tokens; no inspected erratum resolves that wording difference.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: An author correction or archived preprocessing specification would be required to change the canonical 100-word interpretation.

uncertainties.note: The paper does not state which FAISS index variant produced Table 2; its runtime profile uses HNSW while the pinned public snapshot defaults to exhaustive inner-product search.

inclusion.rationale: RAG combines dense retrieval with a pretrained encoder-decoder generator and distinguishes sequence-level from token-level marginalization over retrieved passages. significance.beginner: RAG lets a generator consult retrieved Wikipedia passages rather than relying only on parameters. Its two variants either keep one latent passage for a whole answer or let the document mixture change token by token, and its small index-swap probe demonstrates why external memory can be easier to update than weights.

The 82-item index replacement probe uses one templated class of facts and cannot establish broad temporal updating or deletion of parametric knowledge.

versions.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners

bibliography.citation: T. B. Brown et al., “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners,” in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33, pp. 1877–1901, 2020.
bibliography.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems

versions.notes: The canonical proceedings treatment is a 25-page article plus a separately distributed 32-page supplement. Their visible article pagination controls locators; volume pp. 1877–1901 are bibliographic only. The supplement retains the earlier PF-day conversion error, while arXiv v4 carries the correction.

inclusion.rationale: Brown et al. connect GPT-2-style causal language modeling and Kaplan-era scaling guidance to a 175-billion-parameter family evaluated through explicit zero-, one-, and few-shot text conditioning. The work is retained for its in-context evaluation paradigm, scale study, heterogeneous evidence, and unusually explicit contamination and limitation analysis—not as proof that demonstrations always create new learning or that scale alone explains every result.

significance.beginner: GPT-3 shows that examples can act like temporary instructions: put a few demonstrations in the prompt and the same frozen model may continue the pattern without retraining. The important lesson is conditional, not magical—more scale often widened the benefit of examples, but prompts, tasks, data overlap, and weak spots changed the result.
significance.expert: The study scales a GPT-2-derived causal decoder family from 125M to 175B trainable parameters, adds alternating dense/local sparse attention, samples 300B tokens per model from a quality-weighted five-source mixture, and evaluates zero/one/few-shot conditioning without gradient updates. Interpretation must preserve total versus non-embedding parameter accounts, uniform token budgets despite Kaplan-guided allocation, task-specific scoring and splits, contamination-filter failure, clean-subset limits, internal reporting differences, incomplete artifacts, and separate paper/API/model-card states.

limitations: Text demonstrations change activations rather than parameters; the paper does not establish whether each gain is new task learning, recognition of a pretrained behavior, or another form of conditional adaptation.

Aggregate scaling trends coexist with weak, nonmonotonic, and prompt-sensitive tasks. The comparisons are neither compute matched nor a controlled attribution of every downstream change to parameter count.

Every reported model trains on 300 billion sampled tokens. Kaplan-guided larger-model/fewer-token reasoning is a design rationale, not evidence that each row follows a separate token-optimal allocation.

Training-data provenance is incomplete: the exact 41 Common Crawl shards, classifier, Books1 and Books2 identities, Wikipedia dump, WebText2 reconciliation, prepared-corpus digest, and consolidated rights manifest are unavailable.

A benchmark-decontamination bug left overlap in long documents and books. Heuristic dirty/clean comparisons can contain false positives and distribution shifts and cannot prove absence of memorization.
The zero-, one-, and few-shot comparisons use task-specific prompts, K selection, scoring normalization, generation rules, and a mix of public test and development splits.
The human news-detection result is restricted to selected prompts, article lengths, sampling settings, participant recruitment, and exclusion rules; it is not a general detector-performance claim.
Gender, race, and religion analyses are explicitly preliminary, prompt dependent, and partly confounded by the sentiment tool; they do not establish that scale generally reduces social bias.
Several-thousand-PF-day and 0.4-kWh statements are estimates under paper-specific accounting and do not provide measured electricity, carbon, hardware lifecycle, or serving cost.

The official release snapshot lacks model weights, training or inference code, tokenizer files, the pretraining corpus, full filter implementation, run seeds, and a complete evaluation package; exact reconstruction is not established.

The sources retain visible reporting differences, including 175B versus 174.6B precision, a printed 13B width of 5,140, legacy 200B labels, a Winograd dirty-fraction mismatch, and the proceedings supplement's obsolete PF-day conversion.

ArXiv's license is a non-exclusive distribution grant, no express reusable license was identified in the inspected NeurIPS files, and the initial release repository has no LICENSE; public availability is not represented as general reuse permission.

uncertainties.note: The identities, snapshots, preparation, and rights for Books1, Books2, the English Wikipedia input, and the exact filtered Common Crawl payload remain unresolved.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: An immutable training-corpus manifest with source-level provenance and rights is required.

uncertainties.note: The paper reports WebText2 as 19B available tokens while Kaplan et al. report 22.9B total tokens; no primary record reconciles the processing boundary.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A versioned WebText2 preparation and split manifest is required.

uncertainties.note: The September model card and hosted API describe later model or product states and remain unbound provenance records rather than paper revisions.

versions.notes: The latest 45-page preprint adds the missing leading negative sign to the pairwise reward-model loss on article p. 6. The audited technical substance is otherwise materially stable against version 2.

inclusion.rationale: Stiennon et al. turn pairwise judgments about English summaries into a learned scalar reward and use KL-regularized PPO to update a GPT-style policy at billion-parameter scale. The work is retained as the focused summarization bridge into later instruction-following RLHF, with evaluator scope, length confounding, reward over-optimization, and release boundaries kept visible.

significance.beginner: A model first learns to imitate human-written summaries, then a second model learns which of two summaries people prefer. Reinforcement learning improves the summarizer against that learned score while a tether to the supervised model limits how far it can drift.
significance.expert: The study fine-tunes 1.3B and 6.7B GPT-style decoders on filtered TL;DR data, fits pairwise reward models from 64,832 comparisons, and runs PPO with terminal reward, a log-ratio KL penalty, and a separate value network. Its strongest evidence is human preference under a researcher-defined labeler protocol; corrected-loss, length, domain-transfer, over-optimization, artifact, and rights boundaries remain version-specific.

limitations: The promoted result is a 24–48-token English summarization study on a heavily filtered, relationship-skewed Reddit distribution; it is not a general assistant or universal preference result.
Contractor judgments follow researcher-authored instructions and a small calibration process. Preference labels do not represent every reader, culture, use case, or affected group.
Human-feedback policies learned longer summaries. Length controls reduce the headline preference advantage, and CNN/DM transfer compares substantially different output-length distributions.
The learned reward is an imperfect proxy. Stronger optimization eventually makes the earlier reward model anti-correlate with fresh human judgments.
The study lacks an equal-cost supervised baseline built from equally curated high-quality demonstrations, so it does not isolate feedback format from annotation effort.
Reported results mix exploratory data rounds, changing policies, improved cleaning, and improved hyperparameters rather than one preregistered fixed pipeline.
The 6.7B PPO run required about 320 GPU-days and thousands of labeler hours; the released 1.3B artifacts do not reproduce the full 6.7B result.
The paper, software, feedback data, processed TL;DR corpus, original Reddit text, and CNN/DM material have distinct provenance and rights scopes.

uncertainties.note: ArXiv version 3 corrects the missing negative sign in the pairwise reward-model loss; earlier preprints and the canonical proceedings article retain the erroneous printing.
Exact end-to-end reconstruction of the 6.7B training result is not established by the released 1.3B inference package, feedback data, and paper hyperparameters.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: Versioned pretraining inputs, training code, full run manifests, contractor workflow records, and 6.7B model artifacts would be required.

inclusion.rationale: FLAN makes supervised multitask instruction tuning a direct intervention on a 137B decoder-only language model, evaluates task-family holdouts with separate checkpoints, and isolates dataset diversity, scale, and instruction semantics. Its headline gains are retained with prompt-selection, comparator, contamination, cluster-taxonomy, compute, model-release, and data-rights limits.

significance.beginner: FLAN trains one large language model across many tasks written as natural-language instructions, then tests a separately tuned checkpoint on each withheld kind of task. The paper's visible component document counts sum to about 2.217B rather than the prose's 2.35B, and its selected source-weight description does not fully reconcile with rounded Table 2 weights.

inclusion.rationale: Hoffmann et al. revisit fixed-training-compute allocation with three empirical estimators, expose learning-schedule and scale differences from Kaplan et al., and validate the resulting smaller-model/more-data prescription through the compute-matched Chinchilla–Gopher comparison. The work is retained as a central scaling turn, not as a timeless 20-tokens-per-parameter rule or proof that model size and data should be balanced under every architecture, corpus, objective, hardware, or inference workload.

significance.beginner: A training budget can buy a larger model, more examples, or both. Chinchilla’s lesson is that spending nearly all extra compute on parameters can leave a model undertrained: across this study’s regime, parameters and training tokens rose at roughly the same rate, and a 70B model trained on 1.4T tokens beat the 280B Gopher at matched training compute. That is a bounded empirical result, not a universal recipe.
significance.expert: The study estimates N_opt(C) and D_opt(C) through a training-curve envelope, nine IsoFLOP profiles, and a robust fit L̂(N,D)=E+A/N^α+B/D^β. It contrasts .46–.50 parameter and .50–.54 token exponents with Kaplan’s .73/.27 allocation, counts total-parameter and exact Transformer FLOPs, and validates at 5.76×10^23 FLOPs with a Gopher-derived 70B/1.4T model. Interpretation must preserve schedule matching, dataset and single-epoch scope, only two comparable large runs, curvature, task-protocol differences, no Chinchilla replicate, proprietary artifacts, title and author metadata conflicts, and the 1.3T/1.4T and other reporting discrepancies.

limitations: The fitted frontier minimizes smoothed autoregressive training loss under a fixed training-FLOP budget; it does not jointly optimize inference demand, memory, wall-clock time, energy, carbon, data acquisition, or total lifecycle cost.

The scaling analyses cover dense autoregressive Transformers, the paper's tokenizer, optimizer heuristics, sequence length, MassiveText-derived data, and measured compute range; mixture-of-experts, retrieval, other objectives, modalities, and later architectures require new evidence.
The three estimators share training runs, architectural choices, data, schedules, and a power-law premise, so agreement among them is not three independent replications.
Only Chinchilla and Gopher are comparable at the largest scale, with no intermediate large-scale validation points and no repeated Chinchilla training run.
The paper observes curvature in the high-compute frontier and says the power-law projection may still overestimate optimal large-model size.

The analysis is framed around less than one aggregate epoch, while the 1.4T Chinchilla mixture repeats MassiveWeb about 1.24 times and Wikipedia about 3.40 times; data quality and repeated-data behavior remain unresolved.
The learning-rate cycle must be chosen for the target training horizon. Intermediate points from a longer schedule can overestimate the loss attainable with a matched shorter schedule.
Chinchilla and Gopher differ in size and data exposure but also in optimizer, tokenizer normalization, batch schedule, and sample mixture; downstream comparisons do not isolate token count alone.

Several comparisons reuse evaluation protocols from the Gopher paper, and the paper explicitly says GPT-3 and MT-NLG RACE prompts differ; broad cross-model score comparisons are not uniformly controlled.

The benchmark tables report point estimates without repeated large-model runs, confidence intervals, or task-level significance tests. The abstract’s word “uniformly” exceeds several printed ties or exceptions.

MassiveText, run-level measurements, fitting code, checkpoints, tokenizer assets, and Chinchilla weights are not released; the paper checklist says code and data are proprietary, and the model card says the model will not be public.
The source family contains title, author-form, LaMDA-token, MMLU-rounding, bootstrap-rounding, and 1.3T-versus-1.4T differences that must remain version- and source-bound.

The paper's training FLOPs omit development, evictions, and other inefficiency; the carbon estimate omits embodied hardware and broader project work, and renewable compensation does not mean zero gross emissions.
Continued 62B training changes token count, dataset freshness, source weights, and mixture contents together and does not improve every reported repeated-versus-refreshed comparison.

versions.title: OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models
versions.label: Canonical arXiv version 4

bibliography.citation: S. Zhang et al., “OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models,” arXiv:2205.01068v4, 21 June 2022.

versions.notes: The canonical 30-leaf revision adds the 66B configuration and changes public-release prose and contributor scope from 30B to 66B, but leaves the model-count sentence at eight while Table 1 now contains nine rows. The official 66B checkpoint-and-checksum commit followed on 22 June.

inclusion.rationale: OPT is a pivotal open-checkpoint and operational-transparency branch in the GPT-3-scale lineage. Its main contribution is not a new decoder objective: it attempts a size- and evaluation-aligned replication while releasing code, incident logs, cards, and a scale ladder of weights, with the largest checkpoint gated under restrictive terms. That combination makes access and reproducibility themselves part of the historical record.

significance.beginner: OPT asks what changes when a GPT-3-scale model family becomes inspectable rather than API-only. The smaller and 66B checkpoints, public code, cards, and training logbook widened study access, while 175B remained request-gated and the data stayed unavailable—so “open” must be unpacked artifact by artifact.
significance.expert: OPT largely follows the GPT-3 model, optimization, and prompting frame but changes its corpus and distributed implementation. Its scientific value includes versioned configuration, cross-corpus deduplication, FSDP-plus-tensor-parallel training, disclosed mid-flight interventions, a broad scale ladder, and safety evaluations; its evidentiary value depends on preserving incomplete data provenance, heterogeneous comparisons, restrictive model terms, and internal reporting inconsistencies.

limitations: OPT is a GPT-3-class replication study, not a new Transformer architecture, language-model objective, or instruction-tuned system.
The reported 180B-token corpus, 300B-token schedule, data mixture, filtering, and validation split are not accompanied by an immutable prepared-corpus manifest or distribution package.
OPT-175B training includes unablated restarts and mid-flight learning-rate, clipping, optimizer, loss-scaler, and implementation interventions, so the final trajectory is not one controlled recipe.
Average GPT-3 comparisons combine reconstructed prompts, reported results, and later Davinci API checks; several tasks are unstable, mismatched, excluded, or internally described inconsistently.
The responsible-AI probes are English-heavy, benchmark- and prompt-specific, and sometimes compare against a potentially safety-mediated API rather than the original GPT-3 checkpoint.
Public availability is tiered: checkpoints through 66B are directly listed, while the paper-era 175B path requires approved access and presigned URLs under non-commercial restrictions.
The public code, model weights, paper, logbook, and source datasets have separate licenses and provenance; no one grant covers the complete training and evaluation stack.

uncertainties.note: The paper does not publish source-level token counts or sampling weights for the combined 180B-token corpus, so the exact repetition pattern behind the nominal 300B-token schedule cannot be reconstructed.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: An immutable prepared-corpus manifest with source weights, document and token counts, filters, and per-run sampling logs is required.

uncertainties.note: The launch-day release lacked a public weight manifest, but official 4 and 6 June commits added MD5 identities for the 992 raw OPT-175B shards and the derived eight-part evaluation package; access nevertheless remained controlled.

versions.title: The BigScience ROOTS Corpus: A 1.6TB Composite Multilingual Dataset
versions.label: Combined arXiv version 1

bibliography.citation: H. Laurençon et al., “The BigScience ROOTS Corpus: A 1.6TB Composite Multilingual Dataset,” arXiv:2303.03915v1, 7 March 2023.

versions.notes: The sole arXiv revision is a thirty-six-leaf recombination of the venue article and supplement with an added contents leaf and continuous PDF-viewer pagination. It postdates the proceedings treatment and exposes the complete source package under CC BY 4.0; it is not used to backdate the paper's public chronology.

inclusion.rationale: ROOTS makes multilingual training data and its governance a separate historical object: source discovery, language expertise, source-level traceability, processing, release controls, privacy limitations, and artifact-specific rights are documented rather than collapsed into a model paper's corpus summary. Its importance is this inspectable sociotechnical data pipeline, not a priority claim about multilingual web corpora or participatory research.

significance.beginner: ROOTS shows that a training corpus is a chain of choices made by people: which languages and sources count, how documents are cleaned, what can be redistributed, and which harms remain after filtering. Its three incompatible-looking dataset counts are a practical lesson in asking what exactly was counted.
significance.expert: ROOTS supplies a versioned, source-located account of a 1.6TB composite corpus: community-sourced and OSCAR components, heterogeneous acquisition routes, source- and document-level deduplication, language-conditioned thresholds, limited PII redaction, component-governed release, and tokenizer-fertility analysis. It also exposes reconstruction gaps and value conflicts that aggregate dataset-size reporting obscures.

limitations: The paper reports 252 catalogued sources, 517 datasets after the three acquisition pipelines, 485 non-empty processed datasets in one stage, and 498 constituent Hugging Face datasets, but does not publish a single reconciliation ledger for those scopes.

Only 223 of 498 components were described as directly distributable in the venue paper; the complete prepared corpus, immutable component manifest, and component digests were not supplied in the audited publication bundle.
OSCAR and other web-derived components retain unresolved consent, privacy, representation, and legal questions; the implemented pattern-based redaction is explicitly incomplete.
The descriptive corpus analyses do not isolate how any individual sourcing, filtering, or governance choice changes a trained model's capabilities or harms.

uncertainties.note: The primary paper does not explicitly map its 517 acquisition outputs and 485 non-empty processed datasets onto the final 498 constituent datasets.
The publication identifies a preliminary gated component release but does not provide an immutable full-corpus manifest from which every paper-era component and access condition can be reconstructed.

versions.notes: The canonical 73-leaf revision adds Daniel McDuff to Broader Impacts, repairs the truncation markers in DiaBLa Table 7, and reflows and reorders the multilingual-probing tables, figures, and discussion. The audited scientific values are otherwise retained from version 3.

inclusion.rationale: BLOOM makes a multilingual 176B-scale dense model an unusually inspectable sociotechnical object: target-side documentation ties the model to ROOTS, records architecture and run operations, exposes multiple model scales and checkpoint documentation, and separates a use-restricted weight license from code and paper terms. Its historical value is this joined multilingual, operational, artifact, and governance surface—not a priority claim for decoder-only language modeling, ALiBi, instruction tuning, model cards, or responsible licensing.

significance.beginner: BLOOM shows that one model name can hide several different things: a four-revision paper, six pretrained sizes, a particular 176B training run, intermediate and final checkpoints, a later fine-tuned BLOOMZ derivative, and different permissions for paper, code, weights, and data. Its results also change sharply with prompts, languages, and output handling.
significance.expert: BLOOM supplies a versioned account of ROOTS-conditioned multilingual causal pretraining, ALiBi and embedding-LayerNorm design choices, 3D Megatron-DeepSpeed execution, bfloat16 stability, a 366B-exposure run, heterogeneous prompt-based evaluations, checkpoint-level documentation, carbon scopes, and RAIL-governed model release. The record preserves small-scale ablation limits, paper/config conflicts, mutable model-card drift, BLOOMZ nonidentity, and incomplete byte-identical reconstruction.

limitations: Architecture and objective choices were ablated at 1.3B or 6.7B parameters, and the paper itself questions extrapolation to 176B after a reported outlier-feature phase transition above 6.7B.
The evaluation suite mixes tasks, prompts, languages, shots, metrics, output handling, and external comparator sources; it does not support a prompt-independent or universal performance ranking.

The paper reports about 341B ROOTS corpus tokens and 366B training-token exposures, while paper-era training documentation also uses 350B unique tokens and an unrealized 450B plan; no immutable exposure-by-source ledger reconciles those scopes.

Public code, checkpoints, model cards, and operational notes improve inspection but do not supply the complete prepared training shards, immutable environment, all internal revisions, optimizer-state history, or event logs needed for byte-identical reruns.

The BLOOM RAIL terms restrict specified behaviors and do not transfer the paper's CC BY terms or software licenses to model weights, ROOTS components, third-party datasets, outputs, or downstream systems.

uncertainties.note: Canonical paper Section 3.5 says training used no dropout, while the paper-era public 176B training README says Megatron-LM defaults of 0.1 attention and hidden dropout were inherited and the audited final Slurm file does not override them.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: Resolve with an immutable runtime argument dump or training log bound to the final 176B job.

uncertainties.note: The inspected public sources do not completely reconcile approximately 341B corpus tokens, 350B unique-token wording, 366B realized exposures, and the 410B/450B schedule horizons.
The exact paper-era dependency commits and all prepared data-shard identities are not bound into one public immutable run manifest.

versions.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
versions.label: Canonical ICLR 2023 oral record

bibliography.citation: S. Yao et al., “ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models,” The Eleventh International Conference on Learning Representations, 2023.
bibliography.venue: The Eleventh International Conference on Learning Representations

versions.notes: The official ICLR program supplies canonical title, authors, year, abstract, oral/top-5% status, and a 3 May presentation slot. The venue full text was behind an interactive verification gate during audit, so byte identity with arXiv v3 is not asserted.

inclusion.rationale: ReAct makes environment interaction part of a prompted language-model trajectory by interleaving generated textual thoughts, task actions, and returned observations. It is retained as a bounded bridge from in-context reasoning to explicit action loops across retrieval and simulated environments, not as a general trained-agent release, a proof that visible thoughts faithfully expose hidden reasoning, or a priority claim for language-conditioned control.

significance.beginner: ReAct shows a language model alternating between notes to itself, actions it can send to a tool or environment, and observations returned by that environment. The useful distinction is that a thought only changes the text context, while an action can fetch information or change simulated state; success still depends on the prompt, the allowed actions, the external environment, and the selected model.
significance.expert: ReAct augments a task action space with free-form language traces and prompts frozen PaLM-540B from human trajectories, using dense thought-action-observation alternation for HotpotQA/FEVER and sparse asynchronous thoughts for ALFWorld/WebShop. The record preserves heuristic CoT-SC fallbacks, success-filtered PaLM-8B/62B fine-tuning, prompt-selection and comparator asymmetries, four benchmark environments, visible-trace rather than faithfulness evidence, later GPT-3 code, and separate paper/code/data/model rights.

limitations: The principal experiments use an unreleased PaLM-540B system; the public repository implements later GPT-3 prompting and does not reproduce the complete PaLM environment, generated trajectories, fine-tuning runs, or every benchmark dependency.

HotpotQA, FEVER, ALFWorld, and WebShop use different action spaces, prompt counts, selection rules, metrics, comparators, and external state, so their results do not form one model-only capability scale.
Generated thought text is observable and editable output, not direct evidence that it faithfully reports a model's internal computation or provides a causal explanation of every action.

The strongest ALFWorld figure selects the best of six prompt permutations, the WebShop experiment uses one prompt and a simulated benchmark, and the human-edit result is a single qualitative intervention.
The paper itself reports loops, reasoning errors, uninformative retrieval, long-context limits, and the need for more high-quality annotations and future multi-task or reinforcement learning.
Article, code, PaLM access, GPT-3 service use, embedded data subsets, Wikipedia content, ALFWorld, WebShop, and upstream benchmark rights remain distinct.

uncertainties.note: No immutable public record establishes byte identity between the ICLR-hosted paper and arXiv version 3.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A venue PDF with a stable digest or an official author statement tying it exactly to arXiv v3 is required.

uncertainties.note: The current GitHub repository succeeds the anonymous code URL printed in arXiv v3, but the inspected records do not prove that every file is identical to the paper-time anonymous snapshot.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: An archived anonymous repository tree or signed mapping to a public commit is required.

uncertainties.note: The public repository's summary reports PaLM HotpotQA/FEVER values of 29.4/62.2 and GPT-3 HotpotQA 30.4, while the camera-ready body reports ReAct 27.4/60.9 on its main evaluation and Appendix Table 5 reports 29.4/30.8 on a 500-question HotpotQA subset.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A result manifest binding each displayed number to exact examples, prompts, model snapshots, and evaluation scripts is required.

versions.notes: The 17-leaf ordering manuscript has eight authors and combines the main GPT-J study, additional analysis, prompts, training detail, and DATESET appendix in one file. Its record abstract says “two different search engines,” while the deposited PDF and source enumerate one Atlas question-answering system and one BM25 Wikipedia search system.

versions.title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
versions.label: Canonical NeurIPS 2023 article and supplement

bibliography.citation: T. Schick et al., “Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools,” in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, vol. 36, pp. 68539–68551, 2023.
bibliography.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems

versions.notes: The canonical version adds Eric Hambro, reformats the retained GPT-J study into a 13-leaf article and 10-leaf supplement, moves additional analysis to the supplement, and adds qualitative failure modes plus LLaMA-v1 investigations. The new supplement also identifies GPT-2 as scorer for the original GPT-J-generated data, in tension with the main text's use of GPT-J as the single model M.

inclusion.rationale: Toolformer adds a distinct training route to the retrieval-and-action lane: a causal language model proposes inline textual API calls from a few demonstrations, executes them, keeps calls whose returned result lowers future-token loss, and then learns the retained call/result sequences with ordinary language modeling. It is retained for that self-labeled tool-use mechanism and its evidence that tool value depends on both tool and base model—not as a priority claim for tool use, an autonomous agent, a released model, or a general solution for safe API execution.

significance.beginner: Toolformer turns ordinary text into its own practice material: it proposes places where a tool might help, tries the call, keeps calls that make the next words easier to predict, and studies the edited text. The useful lesson is that a tool is not automatically helpful—a search result can distract a stronger model, and the published system cannot chain calls or revise a query.
significance.expert: Toolformer samples call positions and arguments from GPT-J demonstrations, executes five text-valued tools, filters with a counterfactual weighted future-token loss, merges retained annotations into CCNet, and fine-tunes a causal LM before interrupt-and-inject inference. The audit preserves tool-specific thresholds, heuristics, model swaps, top-rank triggering, one-call evaluation cap, full result envelopes, the GPT-J/GPT-2 scorer contradiction, proceedings-only LLaMA addendum, missing release artifacts, and separate rights.

limitations: The evaluated decoder allows at most one API call per input and the independently sampled training calls do not teach chained or interactive tool use, query revision, browsing, or long-horizon environment control.
API-call triggering is forced whenever the call marker ranks in the top ten, which raises call rates but discards the partial selectivity observed under ordinary greedy decoding.

Training and evaluation use task-specific heuristics, prompts, tool implementations, lenient answer-containment metrics, and live or snapshot-dependent external systems; results are not a model-only measure of general tool competence.

The proceedings supplement contradicts the main single-model notation by identifying GPT-2 as scorer for GPT-J-generated training calls and does not publish a run manifest that resolves the realized scoring path.

The LLaMA addendum shows model-relative utility: Atlas helps selected LAMA tasks, the BM25 search tool reduces all three QA scores, and the calculator study fails to elicit calls from only 401 retained examples.

No official code, generated annotation corpus, Toolformer checkpoint, tokenizer binding, tool snapshot, predictions, seeds, or end-to-end environment was identified in the paper, supplement, proceedings record, or Meta publication page.

The audited tools return text and are read-only retrieval, translation, calendar, or arithmetic functions; the study does not evaluate state-changing APIs, prompt injection, malicious tool output, privacy leakage, permissions, or operational safety.

uncertainties.note: The main method and experimental setup use GPT-J as model M for sampling and loss filtering, while the proceedings supplement says the original calls were generated by GPT-J and scored by GPT-2.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A paper-author clarification or immutable training code and run configuration binding the sampling and scoring checkpoints is required.

uncertainties.note: Appendix B says training uses up to 25,000 examples per API, while the LLaMA addendum reports 32,180 retained QA examples and does not state whether or how that set was capped before training.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A released data manifest or exact training sampler is required to reconcile retained and consumed example counts.

uncertainties.note: The Meta publication page is dated 22 February 2024 and links the canonical paper, but it supplies no independent date for the underlying research or a release artifact.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A dated official release announcement or immutable artifact record is required before assigning a separate model-release event.

versions.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
versions.label: Latest arXiv version 3

bibliography.citation: W. Fedus, B. Zoph, and N. Shazeer, “Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity,” arXiv:2101.03961v3, 16 June 2022.

versions.notes: Version 3 is scientifically aligned with version 2, corrects the Table 9 layer/expert header order, and adds a footnote linking JAX code and all model checkpoints in T5X alongside the TensorFlow implementation. The cited T5X checkpoint release landed two days before this revision.

inclusion.rationale: Switch Transformers fills the sparse-and-efficient architecture lane with a target-documented mechanism: replace selected T5 feed-forward blocks by token-routed expert banks, activate one expert per token, and scale total parameter capacity without proportionally scaling the reported per-sequence FLOPs. It is retained for that conditional-computation design, stability interventions, distributed implementation, and bounded evidence—not because total parameter count equals active computation, every task improves, the largest run is stable, or the release reconstructs every experiment.

significance.beginner: A Switch layer stores many different feed-forward ‘workbenches’ but sends each token to one of them. That makes total capacity grow faster than the work performed on a token, while also introducing a new traffic problem: popular experts overflow and distributed devices must exchange tokens.
significance.expert: Switch Transformer replaces alternating T5 FFNs with top-1 token routing, fixed expert capacity, an auxiliary balancing loss, selective float32 routing, expert-only fine-tuning dropout, and expert/data/model parallelism. The record keeps total parameters, FLOPs per sequence, wall-clock comparisons, token drops, stability, downstream transfer, version corrections, code paths, checkpoints, and rights separate.

limitations: The paper's sparsity is over feed-forward weights, not attention patterns; the standard model retains dense attention and does not solve quadratic long-context attention cost.

Reported total parameters are not active parameters per token. The paper reports FLOPs per sequence and routing/communication costs but does not provide one uniform active-parameter or inference-throughput ledger for every model.
Fixed expert capacity can drop overflow tokens through the residual path; larger capacity spends more memory and compute, and load balancing does not guarantee semantically useful specialization.
Speed claims depend on TPUv3 hardware, device counts, Mesh TensorFlow partitioning, communication, implementation details, batch shape, and the selected perplexity threshold.

Selective precision and smaller initialization stabilize several scales but not Switch-XXL; the larger total-parameter Switch-C is stable while the more compute-intensive Switch-XXL is sometimes unstable.

Upstream perplexity gains do not uniformly translate to downstream reasoning performance, and the paper's largest-model comparisons are preliminary single-value evaluations without a complete repeated-seed uncertainty study.

The post-publication T5X release lists nine converted checkpoints and configurations, but no single immutable manifest binds every paper table to raw predictions, seeds, data order, exact runtime, checkpoint digest, and evaluation output.

uncertainties.note: Canonical JMLR Table 9 and arXiv v2 label the second header block ‘Num. Experts’ then ‘Num Layers’ even though the values are layer counts then expert counts; arXiv v3 reverses the headings without changing the values.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: An official journal erratum would be required to correct the canonical article rather than relying on the later arXiv revision.

versions.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
versions.label: Expanded arXiv version 2

bibliography.citation: DeepSeek-AI, “DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning,” arXiv:2501.12948v2, 4 January 2026.

versions.notes: The 86-leaf revision incorporates the expanded peer-reviewed account and supplement into one arXiv manuscript, adds a long contributor list and extensive training, evaluation, safety, and discussion material, and is not byte-identical to the Nature article-plus-supplement package. Its Open Weights, Code, and Data section retains an unresolved ‘xxx’ placeholder for the claimed SFT/RL-data release.

inclusion.rationale: DeepSeek-R1 fills the bounded reinforcement-learned-reasoning lane with an unusually detailed peer-reviewed account of outcome-verifiable RL, an SFT-free first stage, a separate multistage production model, explicit negative results, and released weights. It is retained for those mechanisms and boundaries—not as proof that visible rationales are faithful, that the base model lacked reasoning traces, that every capability improved, or that public artifacts reconstruct the training run.

significance.beginner: DeepSeek-R1-Zero starts from an already pretrained large model and rewards correct, well-formatted final answers without first teaching worked solutions. The later DeepSeek-R1 adds curated examples, preference rewards, and another RL stage to improve readability and general usefulness, so ‘pure RL’ describes one post-training stage rather than the model’s whole history.
significance.expert: The work applies GRPO with group-normalized outcome rewards and reference-policy KL control to DeepSeek-V3-Base, then builds R1 through cold-start SFT, rule-reward RL, rejection-sampled reasoning/general SFT, and mixed rule/model-reward RL. Interpretation must preserve base-model exposure, stage-specific data and rewards, reward hacking, nonmonotonic evaluation, decontamination limits, distillation identity, mutable artifact releases, and absent run-level reconstruction materials.

limitations: ‘Pure reinforcement learning’ means that DeepSeek-R1-Zero receives no supervised fine-tuning immediately before RL; it still inherits DeepSeek-V3-Base architecture, 14.8-trillion-token pretraining, and whatever human- or model-generated reasoning patterns were present in that corpus.

Rule rewards apply most cleanly to domains with automatically checkable final answers. The paper does not show the same recipe solving open-ended writing, factuality, social judgment, or tool use without learned evaluators or supervised data.
Longer visible reasoning, reflective words, and self-correction-like text do not establish that natural-language rationales faithfully reveal latent computation or that every extra token is useful.

Stage results are nonmonotonic across benchmarks; DeepSeek-R1-Zero exceeds the final model on some reported GPQA and Chinese factual-QA rows, while general instruction-preference gains arrive mainly in later stages.

The reported decontamination removes exact 10-gram matches but explicitly cannot prevent paraphrased or discussed test items from appearing in pretraining; several comparisons also use heterogeneous external or model-judged protocols.
Smaller 7B dense and 16B MoE trials did not obtain meaningful AIME gains and instead lengthened repetitive outputs, so the evidence does not establish base-model-independent effectiveness.

The released repositories and model snapshots do not supply the complete RL/SFT corpora, preference labels, rollouts, data order, seeds, optimizer checkpoints, raw predictions, or one immutable environment and table-to-run ledger.

DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-R1-Zero, the six dense distilled models, their Qwen/Llama bases, DeepSeek-V3 inference code, paper text, datasets, and the later R1-0528 checkpoint carry separate identities and rights.

uncertainties.note: The Nature data-availability statement points to GitHub and Zenodo samples, while the expanded arXiv source says SFT and RL data are released at an unresolved ‘xxx’ and mentions review attachments; no complete public dataset-to-run manifest was identified.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A versioned first-party inventory with stable object identifiers, contents, licenses, and stage/run mappings is required.

uncertainties.note: The supplement's RL-data table lists 17,000 coding items while adjacent prose describes 17,000 algorithm problems plus 8,000 bug-fix items; the scopes are not reconciled.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: An author correction or released row-level manifest must identify whether the table excludes, overlaps, or summarizes the bug-fix subset.

versions.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
versions.label: Latest arXiv version 3

bibliography.citation: R. Rafailov et al., “Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model,” arXiv:2305.18290v3, 29 July 2024.

versions.notes: The latest 27-leaf revision retains version 2's technical text and results. Its source changes only the attribution around the KL-regularized RL objective, adds two references, and repairs punctuation; bundled unused style and old-method files are not additional paper versions.

inclusion.rationale: Rafailov et al. derive a classification-style policy objective for static pairwise preferences from the same KL-regularized reward-maximization formulation used by learned-reward-plus-PPO systems. The work is retained as the direct offline preference-optimization branch, with theorem assumptions, reference-policy dependence, evaluator scope, task-specific comparisons, version corrections, and release boundaries explicit.

significance.beginner: DPO learns from a fixed set of chosen-versus-rejected answers by comparing how much the trainable model, relative to a frozen reference model, favors each answer. It removes a separately trained reward network and PPO update loop, but it does not remove preferences, a reference policy, an implicit reward interpretation, or evaluator choices.
significance.expert: Under a Bradley–Terry or Plackett–Luce preference model, positive-support reference policy, and beta greater than zero, DPO substitutes r(x,y)=beta log(pi/pi_ref)+beta log Z(x) into the KL-regularized optimum so Z cancels in reward differences. The resulting logistic loss trains policy log-ratios on offline pairs; evidence spans controlled sentiment, TL;DR, and one-turn HH with version-specific optimizer, evaluator, comparator, and artifact limits.

limitations: The closed-form optimum is derived for a general non-parametric policy and a specified reward; training a finite neural network on a finite preference sample does not guarantee recovery of that optimum.
The representation theorem assumes beta is positive and the reference policy assigns positive probability to every prompt–completion pair under consideration.
Bradley–Terry and Plackett–Luce treat preferences as generated from scalar reward differences; inconsistent, context-dependent, population-dependent, or intransitive judgments can violate that model.

DPO removes a separately fitted reward network and policy-gradient sampling during fine-tuning, not the earlier cost of generating candidate answers, collecting preferences, training or selecting a reference model, or evaluating outputs.

The three experiments use different model families, datasets, proxy or human labels, evaluators, sampling temperatures, baselines, and maximum scales. They are not one controlled cross-task benchmark.
The controlled sentiment task uses a classifier-generated reward and synthetic preference pairs, so it cannot establish human-alignment quality.

The TL;DR and dialogue headline curves are primarily judged by gpt-4-0314; prompt wording changes judgments, and the small volunteer study is a convenience sample with a STEM and mainly computer-science focus.

The dialogue study has no successful matched in-study PPO baseline: a third-party 6B PPO checkpoint did not beat the 2.8B base under the authors' attempted prompting and temperatures, so Best-of-128 is used only as a rough PPO-level proxy.
The CNN/DailyMail transfer table uses one task shift, two inherited sampling temperatures, the same modified GPT-4 prompt, and no reported human validation or uncertainty intervals.
Reward over-optimization, use of additional unlabeled prompts, and scaling beyond models up to 6B remain open in the paper rather than demonstrated advantages.

The public reference repository postdates arXiv v1, its initial release contained a loss-masking bug fixed eight days later, and its paper-era tree does not release the exact sentiment or TL;DR pipelines, DPO checkpoints, raw judgments, or a complete table-to-run ledger.

The arXiv manuscripts use CC BY 4.0 and the reference code uses Apache 2.0; model checkpoints, datasets, Reddit text, Anthropic data, GPT-4 service outputs, dependencies, and third-party baselines retain separate identities and terms.

uncertainties.note: All three arXiv PDFs and source packages plus the canonical article and supplement were compared. Version 2 contains substantive framing, derivation, optimizer, and experiment-detail changes; version 3 is citation-level.
The canonical supplement prints Adam while arXiv versions 2–3 print RMSprop; the inspected primary records do not identify which optimizer produced every reported run.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: Immutable experiment configurations and optimizer-state checkpoints mapped to each result would be required to resolve the run-level optimizer identity.

uncertainties.note: No inspected first-party artifact provides all trained policies, preference examples after processing, raw GPT-4 and human judgments, seeds, environments, and exact result scripts.
uncertainties.resolutionCondition: A versioned release with complete data manifests, checkpoints, predictions, evaluator outputs, run configurations, and environment locks would be required for end-to-end reconstruction.

ideas.name: Text as a dependent sequence
ideas.description: Adjacent symbol classes in observed text can have different conditional frequencies than independence would predict.

uncertainties.note: The opening treatment is intentionally limited to the vowel/consonant abstraction used in the 1913 study.

ideas.name: Language as a conditional stochastic source
ideas.description: A discrete language source emits successive symbols according to probabilities that may depend on preceding choices.

ideas.name: Neural next-character probability modeling
ideas.description: A neural predictor maps a bounded character context to estimates of the next-character distribution, allowing contexts absent from a literal lookup table to share parameters.

uncertainties.note: The early Schmidhuber implementations use squared-error training plus sum normalization, whereas ByteNet uses an autoregressive softmax decoder. This shared character-level idea does not imply an identical objective or architecture.

ideas.name: Probability-driven lossless text coding
ideas.description: Encoder and decoder run the same sequential probability predictor so Huffman or arithmetic coding can assign shorter descriptions to more likely next characters while preserving exact recovery.

ideas.name: Neural misprediction-residual coding
ideas.description: A neural predictor selects one deterministic next character, while only mistakes and the lengths of correct runs are retained before a conventional lossless coder is applied.

uncertainties.note: This longer-manuscript-only method is kept separate from Huffman and arithmetic probability coding because it records deterministic prediction errors and explicitly does not use all conditional-probability information.

ideas.name: Entropy as sequence uncertainty
ideas.description: Conditional entropy quantifies average uncertainty about a next event when contextual information is known.

ideas.name: Increasing-order language approximation
ideas.description: Successively longer conditional contexts can produce samples with more of a language’s local statistical structure.

uncertainties.note: Order labels in the paper are preserved alongside explicit context length because they differ from some modern conventions.

ideas.name: Contextual next-symbol prediction
ideas.description: The predictability of the next character can be studied while the correct preceding text remains visible.

ideas.name: Prediction-based entropy bounds
ideas.description: The rank frequencies of next-character predictions can be related to upper and lower bounds on conditional entropy.

ideas.name: Language-model-guided decoding
ideas.description: A decoder can rank candidate word sequences by combining their language-model probability with the likelihood of the observed signal.

ideas.name: Corpus-estimated language model
ideas.description: A structured sequence model can obtain transition probabilities from counts over a domain corpus.

ideas.name: Sparse language-model estimation
ideas.description: A finite sample can leave plausible sequence transitions with zero observed or expected counts, so an estimated probability of zero need not mark an impossible transition.

ideas.name: Interpolated transition estimation
ideas.description: A transition estimate can blend a detailed distribution with a more broadly tied distribution, with the mixing weight reflecting their relative reliability.

ideas.name: Deleted estimation
ideas.description: A block is evaluated as if unseen while estimation is intended to rely on retained observations, making the tuning target resemble future prediction more closely than training-data fit; practical shortcuts can retain implicit full-data dependence.

ideas.name: Word-trigram language modeling
ideas.description: A corpus-derived trigram model assigns probabilities to local three-word patterns, but finite training data leave many patterns unobserved even at million-word scale.

uncertainties.note: The idea is scoped to the chapter’s Laser Patent Text example and is not treated as evidence about unrestricted corpora.

ideas.name: Frequency-of-frequencies discounting
ideas.description: Counts of how many event types occur once, twice, and so on can adjust unreliable low counts and estimate how much total probability should remain for unseen events.

uncertainties.note: Katz attributes the adjusted-count estimator to Turing through Good’s 1953 paper; the corpus does not treat it as Katz’s invention.

ideas.name: Recursive m-gram backoff
ideas.description: A higher-order m-gram model can use a seen-event estimate directly and send unseen events to a normalized lower-order distribution. Katz makes that estimator recursive with an explicit reserved-mass calculation; Kneser and Ney preserve the seen/unseen structure while redesigning the fallback distribution.

uncertainties.note: In Katz’s estimator, this is a zero-estimate gate, not interpolation across all orders; α rescales the lower-order distribution over eligible unseen continuations to the reserved mass β̃ rather than acting as a convex mixture weight.

The papers reuse Greek letters for different quantities: Katz’s α is a lower-order multiplier and β̃ is reserved mass, whereas Kneser and Ney’s α is the seen-event estimate, β is the fallback distribution, and γ is its normalizer.

ideas.name: Context-diversity backoff distributions
ideas.description: A lower-order distribution can depend on how many distinct detailed contexts contain the observed continuation, or on how many such context–continuation events are singletons, rather than on the continuation’s raw token frequency. The original paper uses it for backoff; later work also interpolates it into seen-event estimates.

uncertainties.note: The distinct-context equation is the original paper’s marginal-constraint backoff distribution; later interpolated and modified Kneser–Ney estimators add mechanisms not present in this record.

ideas.name: Interpolated Kneser–Ney smoothing
ideas.description: A discounted higher-order n-gram estimate is recursively added to a scaled continuation-based lower-order distribution for every continuation, so lower-order evidence contributes to both seen and unseen events.

uncertainties.note: Interpolation is a later formulation: the 1995 Kneser–Ney paper applies its optimized lower-order distribution through a seen/unseen backoff gate.

ideas.name: Modified Kneser–Ney count-dependent discounts
ideas.description: Each n-gram order can use separate absolute discounts for events observed once, twice, and three or more times, with the interpolation weight returning the total removed mass through the continuation distribution.

uncertainties.note: The three discount tiers, interpolation choice, and parameter-estimation choice remain separate properties; “modified Kneser–Ney” must not be reduced to any one of them.
The fixed three-discount equations cite Klaus Ries through personal communication, and the journal article reports an independent two-discount proposal by Ney, Martin, and Wessel 1997.

ideas.name: Neural factorization of joint distributions
ideas.description: An ordered product of normalized conditional distributions is parameterized by a constrained neural network whose deterministic hidden units can share computation across several conditionals.

uncertainties.note: The hidden units are deterministic shared computations, not latent random variables; normalization comes from the product of normalized conditionals.

The precursor’s suggestion to represent large-domain values such as words with low-dimensional features is not treated as an implemented language model or as priority evidence for jointly learned word embeddings.

ideas.name: Low-dimensional feature encoding for large domains
ideas.description: Values of a large categorical domain can be represented through multiple low-dimensional features before applying a joint-distribution estimator; in the audited precursor this is a proposal for text, not an implemented or learned representation.

uncertainties.note: The record preserves the paper’s proposed encoding bridge without treating it as experimental language-model evidence or as priority evidence for learned word representations.

ideas.name: Jointly learned word representations
ideas.description: A shared lookup table maps each word type to a continuous vector, and those vectors are optimized together with the probability model rather than supplied as fixed external features.

uncertainties.note: The paper describes learned continuous word features and distributed representations; the atlas uses modern embedding terminology only as explanatory interface language, not as a quotation or priority claim.

ideas.name: Fixed-window feed-forward neural language modeling
ideas.description: A feed-forward network predicts the next word from a fixed window of shared word vectors, optionally combining a nonlinear hidden path with a direct input-to-output path.

ideas.name: Full-vocabulary neural normalization
ideas.description: One score per vocabulary item is exponentiated and normalized into a next-symbol distribution, coupling every training example to the full output vocabulary.

uncertainties.note: Mikolov et al. normalize retained word types plus one rare-word bucket, then divide that bucket’s probability uniformly among the merged rare types; this is not one separately learned output for every original rare type.

ideas.name: Class-factored neural output normalization
ideas.description: A word probability is decomposed into the probability of its assigned class and its probability within that class, reducing the number of output scores evaluated for each history.

uncertainties.note: The 2012 paper evaluates fixed word classes and discusses the square-root class-count heuristic; this idea does not imply a learned hierarchy or a modern approximate-softmax method.

ideas.name: Shortlist hybrid neural language modeling
ideas.description: A neural distribution is normalized over a frequent-word shortlist and scaled by the backoff model’s total shortlist mass, while the backoff model retains the remaining vocabulary probability.

uncertainties.note: The selected system is not a fixed linear mixture across the full vocabulary: it preserves a history-dependent shortlist mass taken from the backoff model.

ideas.name: Context-cached neural language-model decoding
ideas.description: When a decoder sequentially requests many word probabilities for the same history, the outputs already produced by one neural forward pass can be reused across those requests.

ideas.name: Neural and count-model mixtures
ideas.description: A neural next-word distribution can be linearly mixed with an interpolated n-gram distribution so their different generalization behavior contributes to one normalized predictor.

uncertainties.note: The evidence is paper-specific: Bengio et al. use fixed equal-weight neural/interpolated-trigram mixtures; Mikolov et al. report RNN/backoff weights of 0.75/0.25 plus RNN ensembles; and Sundermeyer et al. separately tune a Kneser–Ney/LSTM interpolation whose components use more than four billion versus 27 million training words. None of these results implies that mixtures always improve either component.

ideas.name: Learned distributed representations for symbols
ideas.description: A system can learn multi-unit internal patterns for otherwise discrete symbols so task-relevant regularities are encoded across several units rather than supplied as hand-written symbolic features.

uncertainties.note: This shared idea records a broad representation principle. It does not equate Hinton’s role-specific family codes, Elman’s context-dependent hidden states, Miikkulainen and Dyer’s task-learned global word-type patterns, and Bengio’s static jointly learned word lookup rows.

ideas.name: Similarity-based generalization in learned representation space
ideas.description: Learned internal geometry can expose task-relevant similarities so a model’s behavior transfers among structurally related cases rather than depending only on exact symbolic identity.

uncertainties.note: The Hinton evidence is restricted to two small isomorphic family graphs and four withheld facts; it is not broad semantic or cross-domain transfer evidence.

The Miikkulainen–Dyer evidence is restricted to supervised case-role and stereotyped script tasks; its similarity and cloning results do not establish portable word semantics or open-domain generalization.

ideas.name: Simple recurrent context memory
ideas.description: A copy of the previous hidden activation is supplied as context for the next step, making current state and output depend jointly on the current input and an iterated summary of prior processing.

uncertainties.note: The copied hidden-to-context links are fixed at 1.0; this idea must not be rendered as though every recurrent connection is learned or the paper trained with full backpropagation through time.
Miikkulainen and Dyer explicitly reuse Elman-style copied context, but recurrent FGREP predicts a stationary case-role target rather than the next word.

ideas.name: Constant-error recurrent memory
ideas.description: A recurrent cell preserves internal state and backward error along a fixed unit-weight self-connection, creating a path that avoids exponential decay or growth while that path remains active.

uncertainties.note: A protected error path is a local architectural property, not a guarantee that training will learn arbitrary long-range dependencies; both promoted works retain explicit task and evidence limits.

ideas.name: Gated recurrent memory access
ideas.description: Learned multiplicative controls regulate whether candidate information enters recurrent state, whether prior state is retained, and whether stored state affects cell output; the distinct gate and feedback mechanisms remain separately traceable.

uncertainties.note: The 1995/1997 version has input and output gates only. The 1999/2000 work adds learned retention, and the 2002 work adds cell-state-to-gate feedback; neither mechanism is attributed backward.

ideas.name: Adaptive recurrent state retention
ideas.description: A learned sigmoid gate multiplies the previous recurrent cell state, allowing data-dependent retention, gradual decay, or reset instead of a permanently fixed self-weight or an externally supplied boundary reset.

uncertainties.note: The 1999 report, ICANN paper, and 2000 journal article are grouped as versions of one work, but their exact equations, experiment coverage, weight counts, lag descriptions, and training means are not assumed interchangeable.
This mechanism controls activation-state retention; it is not parameter-level protection against catastrophic forgetting.

ideas.name: Cell-state-to-gate feedback
ideas.description: Learned peephole connections expose protected cell state directly to its gates, so input and forget decisions can inspect prior state and output decisions can inspect newly updated state even when ordinary cell output is closed.

uncertainties.note: The 2002 equations use prior state for input and forget gates and newly updated state for the output gate. Sundermeyer 2012 displays state-to-gate links but does not reproduce that update order, so implementation identity is not inferred.

ideas.name: Task-learned global distributed word lexicon
ideas.description: Backpropagated task error can update one stored distributed pattern per word and reuse that shared pattern as input, output, and inter-module communication across several supervised language-processing tasks.

uncertainties.note: The stored word pattern is global within DISPAR, but its geometry is learned for the supervised tasks and is not a context-dependent token representation or a word vector trained by language-model likelihood.

ideas.name: Modular recurrent neural language processing
ideas.description: Several recurrent networks can specialize in sentence parsing, story parsing, story generation, and sentence generation while communicating through a compatible learned lexicon and explicit case-role or script structures.

uncertainties.note: The modules are separately supervised with compatible targets and correct intermediate lexical patterns during training; the corpus does not describe DISPAR as an end-to-end learned pipeline.

ideas.name: One-hot neural bigram language modeling
ideas.description: A one-hot current-word input can feed a full-vocabulary affine softmax directly, making the network a normalized bigram estimator with no hidden representation and no context beyond one word.

uncertainties.note: The evaluated system contains no hidden units or learned word vectors; calling it neural records its optimization and softmax parameterization, not distributed representation learning.

ideas.name: Early stopping as implicit neural bigram smoothing
ideas.description: Selecting a direct bigram network before full training convergence can regularize sparse word-pair estimates; an exact count-dependent interpolation is derived only for a separate linear squared-error surrogate, while the actual softmax network's smoothing form remains unknown.

uncertainties.note: The corpus does not transfer equations (5.1)–(5.3) from the linear, no-bias, squared-error analysis to the implemented softmax likelihood model.

ideas.name: Next-item prediction as a training task
ideas.description: The observed next element supplies a local target, and pressure to predict it can make hidden state encode regularities in the preceding sequence.

uncertainties.note: For Elman’s lexical experiment this objective uses unnormalized output activations on generated sentences; it is not a softmax language-model likelihood or perplexity objective.
Mikolov et al. instantiate the next-word objective as a normalized vocabulary distribution trained with cross-entropy, but propagate only the current-step error in the main experiments.

ideas.name: Recurrent neural word language modeling
ideas.description: A recurrent hidden state combines the current word with the previous state to parameterize a normalized next-word distribution, allowing history to enter through repeated state updates rather than an explicit fixed window.

uncertainties.note: Recurrence removes an explicit finite input window but does not guarantee usable long-range memory; the target paper explicitly reports that its simple model did not capture truly long context.

ideas.name: Online neural language-model adaptation
ideas.description: A trained neural language model can continue stochastic-gradient updates while processing an ordered test sequence, adapting its parameters to recent text in a cache-like continuous space.

uncertainties.note: The method assumes locally coherent test order; the paper’s WSJ evaluation sentences are not consecutive, and its dynamic model is worse than the static model on that split.

ideas.name: Emergent contextual lexical structure
ideas.description: Hidden states induced by prediction over controlled word sequences can cluster by generator-defined lexical roles even though the input vectors themselves carry no category or meaning labels.

uncertainties.note: The plotted type averages can reflect category-dependent preceding contexts; the paper’s described token-level check is not displayed and supplies no quantitative cluster metric.

ideas.name: Character-level recurrent sequence generation
ideas.description: A recurrent model assigns a normalized probability to each next symbol from the preceding sequence and can feed sampled symbols back as inputs to generate variable-length character streams.

uncertainties.note: The paper evaluates both character and word prediction on Penn Treebank, but this idea names the character-level generative path; it does not imply coherent long-form generation.

ideas.name: Mixture-density handwriting generation
ideas.description: A recurrent network parameterizes a normalized mixture of correlated bivariate Gaussians for the next pen displacement together with a Bernoulli pen-lift probability, supporting likelihood training and stochastic trajectory generation.

uncertainties.note: The continuous density models the next pen offset and lift event; it does not transcribe characters, provide a calibrated legibility score, or isolate visual quality from sampling choices.

ideas.name: Monotonic Gaussian-mixture sequence window
ideas.description: A recurrent state emits positive amplitudes and widths plus cumulative positive location increments for Gaussian windows over an input sequence, yielding a differentiable soft read whose centers can move only forward.

uncertainties.note: The weights are positive but unnormalized, and the paper describes them as a window, window weight, or convolutional mechanism rather than attention.

Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio later compare this monotonic construction directly with weights over every source annotation; that comparison supports a lineage edge without proving derivation or sole priority.

ideas.name: Fixed-vector neural sequence transduction
ideas.description: A recurrent encoder maps a variable-length source sequence into one fixed-dimensional final representation, and a separate recurrent decoder uses that representation to produce a possibly different-length target sequence.

uncertainties.note: Fixed refers to the representation’s dimensionality, not to padded or fixed input length. Both audited decoders condition on one global source summary rather than revisiting individual encoder positions.

The architecture is a plausible information bottleneck, not a universal failure condition. Bahdanau supplies a scoped matched-family comparison and descriptive length curves, but attention, bidirectionality, and capacity change together; Sutskever’s source-reversal result remains an explicit counter-boundary.

ideas.name: Source-conditioned autoregressive decoding
ideas.description: A conditional target-sequence probability is factorized into normalized next-symbol distributions that depend on the source representation and the previously generated target prefix, with an end symbol defining variable output length.

uncertainties.note: The training factorization and approximate search procedure are distinct: a normalized conditional model does not make left-to-right beam search an exact solution to maximum-probability decoding.

ideas.name: Reset–update gated recurrence
ideas.description: A recurrent hidden unit uses a reset gate inside its candidate-state computation and an update gate to mix the preceding state with that candidate, allowing different units to adapt their effective timescales.

uncertainties.note: The paper calls this a new hidden unit rather than ‘GRU’; the atlas does not backdate later terminology or claim sole priority. Gate labels are version- and paper-specific: Cho’s canonical equation weights old state by z and candidate by 1−z, while Bahdanau’s appendix weights old state by 1−z and candidate by z.

The main v3/proceedings equation applies the reset vector before the recurrent matrix multiplication; v1 and the official attachment retain an older componentwise placement and are kept version-bound.

ideas.name: Decoder-conditioned soft attention
ideas.description: At each target step, a learned feedforward score compares the preceding decoder state with every source annotation; a source-position softmax produces differentiable weights whose weighted sum is a step-specific context vector.

uncertainties.note: The paper calls the component a feedforward alignment model and attention mechanism; the atlas describes the additive score composition without backdating later “additive attention” taxonomy as the paper’s own label.
Soft weights are trainable internal quantities over every source position, not a supervised word-alignment posterior or a guaranteed causal explanation.

ideas.name: Bidirectional source annotations
ideas.description: A forward recurrent network and a backward recurrent network are concatenated at each source position, so every position-wise annotation summarizes both preceding and following source context.

uncertainties.note: The encoder requires the complete source sequence before both directional annotations are available; the paper does not claim streaming translation.
The claim that each annotation concentrates around its own word follows the authors’ recency intuition rather than a measured locality ablation.

ideas.name: Fixed-vector source-summary bottleneck
ideas.description: Using one fixed-dimensional source summary for every target step may make it difficult for a sequence model to retain and retrieve all information needed for long inputs.

uncertainties.note: This is the paper’s conjectured diagnosis, not a universal theorem or an isolated causal result; the reported comparison changes attention, encoder directionality, and capacity together.
Each attention context cᵢ remains fixed-dimensional. The change is from one global summary reused at every target step to a fresh weighted retrieval over position-wise annotations.

ideas.name: Neural phrase-pair scoring
ideas.description: A conditional neural sequence score for each source–target phrase pair is added as a feature to a conventional log-linear phrase-based translation system rather than replacing its decoder or phrase table.

uncertainties.note: Generated phrase samples demonstrate that the conditional model can emit candidates, but full phrase-table replacement and direct sentence translation remain future work in this paper.
