claims.statement: T0 samples datasets proportionally while capping any dataset above 500,000 examples at 500000 divided by its template count, packs 1,024-token inputs and 256-token targets into batches of 1,024 sequences or 2²⁰ input tokens, and trains with Adafactor at learning rate 10⁻³ and dropout 0.1. Checkpoints are selected only with validation splits of training datasets.

evidence.support: Reports the sampling cap, lengths, packing, batch, optimizer, learning rate, dropout, and selection data.
States that checkpoint 12,200 was selected and all models were fine-tuned for 12,200 steps in version 1.
Restates 12,200 fine-tuning steps and bf16 activations for the released model.

claims.statement: For classification, T0 ranks candidate target strings by unnormalized sequence likelihood. It performs no held-out development-set prompt selection and reports the median and interquartile range across all eligible prompts, usually on validation splits; BIG-bench uses one maintainer prompt per task.

evidence.support: Defines candidate scoring, absence of length normalization and prompt selection, splits, and median/IQR reporting.

limitations: Unnormalized sequence likelihood can favor shorter options, and a finite prompt pool does not sample all valid phrasings.

claims.statement: Table 6 reports median T5+LM→T0 accuracy gains on all 11 held-out results: WSC 57.69→64.42, Winogrande 50.71→60.46, ANLI R1/R2/R3 32.85→44.70, 32.90→39.40, and 33.75→42.42, CB 33.93→78.57, RTE 51.81→81.23, COPA 55.00→90.79, HellaSwag 27.73→33.65, Story Cloze 48.85→94.71, and WiC 50.24→57.21. T0 matches or exceeds all displayed GPT-3 sizes on 9 of 11, except Winogrande and HellaSwag.

evidence.support: States improvement on all 11 and the 9/11 GPT-3 comparison.

limitations: The paper reports no repeated training runs or formal significance tests, and GPT-3 uses a different prompt-aggregation protocol.

claims.statement: Across 14 selected BIG-bench tasks, at least one T0 variant exceeds every displayed diagnostic language-model baseline on 13 tasks; StrategyQA is the exception. The winning variant can differ by task, and T0, T0+, and T0++ have different supervised mixtures.

evidence.support: Reports the 13-of-14 comparison and the StrategyQA exception across variants.

limitations: This is a per-task best-of-variants statement over a selected 14-task subset, not one model beating all baselines on the entire BIG-bench collection.

claims.statement: Moving from one random original-task prompt to 5.7 original prompts per dataset improves the held-out median on 8 of 11 results and shrinks IQR on 7; moving from 5.7 to 8.03 prompts including non-original tasks improves median on 9 and shrinks IQR on 8. Increasing dataset configurations 39→49→55 improves all five NLI medians at each step but shrinks IQR on only 1 of 5 and then 2 of 5.

evidence.support: Reports the p and d conditions and counts of median and IQR improvements.

claims.statement: In an RTE API check, the Brown-style prompt scores 58.8% rather than the published 63.5%, while nine alternative prompts have median 52.96 and IQR 1.28. The authors cannot verify that API davinci is identical to the 175B GPT-3 artifact, and the main comparison contrasts GPT-3's single reported prompt with T0's prompt median.

evidence.support: Reports the ten-prompt RTE check, median, IQR, published value, and API-model identity caveat.

limitations: One API task cannot calibrate all imported GPT-3 rows, and API state may have changed after the original paper.

claims.statement: T0 describes FLAN as concurrent work with largely the same broad method but different prompt diversity, scale, and holdout design. On common datasets T0 is better on CB and RTE, similar on Story Cloze and COPA, and worse on Winogrande and ANLI; removing instructions raises HellaSwag's median from 33.65 to 57.93 and gives Winogrande 62.15, so instruction semantics are not uniformly beneficial.

evidence.support: Calls FLAN concurrent, enumerates protocol and result differences, and reports the instructionless HellaSwag and Winogrande ablation.

limitations: T0++ has more supervised task exposure than T0, and the paper treats architecture/objective and prompt diversity as possible explanations rather than established causes.

claims.statement: An exact suffix-array audit searches groups of 16 C4 tokens and reports matches including HellaSwag 912/10,000, RTE hypotheses 156/3,000, RTE premises 329/3,000, ANLI premises 337/1,000, and Winogrande 0/1,767. The authors flag HellaSwag's 9.12% and RTE-hypothesis 5.2% as potentially problematic and omit LAMBADA from the main matrix because format and pretraining differences confound comparison.

evidence.support: Defines the 16-token method, enumerates overlaps, and identifies potentially problematic rates.
Explains why LAMBADA is separated from the main held-out comparison and reports format-sensitive results.

limitations: Exact lexical matching is not semantic leakage detection, can over-count longer overlapping blocks, does not audit cross-task supervision or BIG-bench, and is not converted into a causal score correction.

claims.statement: The official release supplies training, evaluation, and inference code, PromptSource tooling, materialized P3 data, and six linked T0-family checkpoints. Paper Table 5 lists 39 base T0 configurations including TyDiQA, while the paper-era registry has 38 BASE rows and no TyDiQA. Apache declarations cover the inspected repositories, the pinned T0 model card, and aggregate P3 artifact but do not establish rights for every upstream dataset; Story Cloze separately requires approved access.

claims.statement: The paper estimates about 270 TPU-v3-512 hours and 8.9 tCO2e for all reported experiments, while a single T0 run is about 27 hours and 0.9 tCO2e; evaluation and preprocessing are additional. It excludes some harmful datasets but explicitly says the models are not bias-free, reports problematic generations and gender-bias probes, and notes that zero-shot T0 remains behind task-specific fine-tuning.

claims.statement: The Gopher preprint family has two arXiv manuscripts: a 118-page version 1 submitted 8 December 2021 and a 120-page version 2 submitted 21 January 2022. Canonical v2 preserves the printed 2021-12-08 manuscript date but revises scaling language, qualifies TruthfulQA with protocol ablations, relabels a supposedly factual dialogue as mixed factuality, adds raw Winogender values and another dialogue, and changes contact and copyright details. The hash-recorded DeepMind launch PDF inspected on 6 September 2026 is substantively v1-equivalent rather than a third version.

evidence.support: The aggregate record supplies both immutable version timestamps and the current 120-page comment; the immutable PDF records supply the version-specific page counts.

evidence.support: The ordering manuscript prints its 2021-12-08 date, original corresponding-author details, and 2021 DeepMind copyright state.
Version 1 makes the broader claim that smaller models often outperform larger models across the low-gain categories.
Version 1 labels the cell-biology exchange an example of factual dialogue.
Version 1 presents the cross-family comparison without the later task-formulation ablation.
Version 1 reports the Winogender figure and prose without the raw-value table added in version 2.

evidence.support: The canonical revision retains the 2021-12-08 manuscript date while changing corresponding-author and copyright details.
Version 2 removes the broader claim about smaller models outperforming larger ones across the low-gain categories.
Version 2 relabels and explains the cell-biology exchange as mixed factuality.
Version 2 qualifies the cross-family comparison by task setup and adds the task-formulation ablation.
Version 2 adds a raw-number table beside the Winogender analysis.
Version 2 adds a second cell-biology dialogue labeled semi-factual.
The source diff isolates substantive text and figure changes from PDF production differences.
The hash-recorded author-hosted payload has the v1-era title-page state and lacks the arXiv side banner; full-text comparison recorded in the source metadata bounds the v1-equivalence inference.

limitations: The unchanged manuscript date printed in v2 is not evidence that the January revision existed in December, and the launch mirror's different PDF bytes do not by themselves define a distinct manuscript.
Version 2 contains unresolved citation markers introduced by additions, so canonical means latest identified manuscript rather than typographically flawless artifact.

claims.statement: The family contains 44M, 117M, 417M, 1.4B, 7.1B, and nominal 280B autoregressive Transformer language models; the largest is Gopher. Gopher uses 80 layers, 128 heads, key/value width 128, model width 16,384, and feed-forward width four times model width. The target says it uses the Radford et al. 2019 architecture with RMSNorm replacing LayerNorm and Dai et al. relative positional encoding replacing absolute positions, plus a 32,000-item SentencePiece vocabulary with byte fallback.

locator.label: Model family, dimensions, and named architecture changes

evidence.support: The canonical paper names the six scales, identifies Gopher, prints every listed dimension, and directly attributes the base architecture and relative-position scheme.

limitations: The Gopher paragraph says autoregressive Transformer; decoder-only continuity is bounded to its explicit adoption of the GPT-2 report's architecture rather than treated as a new invention.
The edge from Transformer-XL carries relative-position scoring only, not segment recurrence, a hidden-state cache, or Transformer-XL benchmark results.
The paper's 280B label is nominal; this claim does not independently reconstruct an exact trainable-parameter inventory.

claims.statement: Every family member trains for 300B tokens with a 2,048-token context and Adam. Gopher uses a peak learning rate of 4×10^-5 after 1,500 warmup steps from 10^-7, a tenfold cosine decay, a batch that grows from 3M to 6M tokens, global gradient clipping at 0.25, and bfloat16 parameters and activations updated with stochastic rounding.

locator.label: Family training schedule and Gopher-specific hyperparameters

evidence.support: The canonical methods paragraph and model table state the common token/context budget and each Gopher setting.

limitations: The sweep does not isolate parameter count: depth, width, head count, key/value size, learning rate, batch size, precision regime, and total compute change with scale.
The paper subsequently reports that stochastic rounding does not fully recover mixed-precision performance.

claims.statement: The authors built the training and evaluation codebase with JAX and Haiku and used TPUv3 chips. Gopher's half-precision parameters plus single-precision Adam state occupy 2.5 TiB, so training partitions optimizer state, applies model and data parallelism within TPU pods, rematerializes activations, and pipelines across pods. The 6M-token configuration uses 4,096 chips; its accelerator-time breakdown assigns 51% to linears, 8% attention, 3% optimizer, 7% model parallelism, 17% rematerialization, 9% pipelining, and 5% other work.

locator.label: Software stack, state footprint, and parallel topology

evidence.support: The methods section names JAX, Haiku, TPUv3, the 2.5 TiB state footprint, and each parallelism mechanism.
The appendix prints the chip count, 6M-batch boundary, and percentage breakdown.

limitations: The percentages are rounded and the 3M-token Gopher batch has roughly doubled optimizer and pipeline contributions rather than the same breakdown.
Named libraries and topology are not a released paper-specific implementation or complete environment lock.

claims.statement: MassiveText combines MassiveWeb, books, C4, news, GitHub, and Wikipedia. Table 2 reports 506B, 560B, 182B, 676B, 422B, and 4B SentencePiece tokens respectively and samples them for Gopher at 48%, 27%, 10%, 10%, 3%, and 2%. The component token counts sum to 2.35T, and the 300B-token Gopher run consumes about 12.8% of that aggregate under nonuniform sampling.

locator.label: MassiveText component sizes and sampling weights

evidence.support: The canonical composition table and surrounding prose state every component, token count, sampling weight, total, and seen-token fraction.

limitations: Twelve-point-eight percent is an aggregate comparison, not a uniform fraction of each component: source-specific resampling can repeat or omit examples.
The displayed document counts sum to about 2.217B rather than the prose's 2.35B, which may depend on unreported unrounded counts.
Appendix A's selected 50/30/10/10 split multiplied by 95% does not fully reconcile with every rounded Table 2 weight.

claims.statement: To form a 2,048-token training sequence, the pipeline selects a document, crops at most 15 times the target length in UTF-8 bytes, tokenizes with beginning- and end-of-document markers, concatenates ten crops because most documents are short, keeps each full 2,048-token block, discards the short tail, then source-weights, shuffles, and batches the examples.

evidence.support: The appendix enumerates cropping, boundary tokens, ten-document concatenation, splitting, tail discard, mixture sampling, shuffling, and batching.

limitations: The prose gives an algorithmic description but no released implementation, random seed, exact document-order manifest, or prepared sequence hashes.

claims.statement: MassiveWeb receives explicit-content filtering through Google SafeSearch, custom HTML extraction, heuristic quality filters, and repetitive-text removal. Document deduplication combines exact matching with punctuation-insensitive, whitespace-normalized MinHash over 13-grams and removes one document when estimated Jaccard similarity exceeds 0.8; selected test-set filtering uses the same 13-gram and threshold scheme.

locator.label: MassiveText filtering, deduplication, and test-overlap pipeline

evidence.support: The appendix diagrams and specifies the stages, normalization, MinHash representation, 0.8 threshold, and test-filter reuse.

limitations: Page 39 says all subsets are deduplicated and its diagram depicts deduplication broadly, while footnote 14 on page 41 explicitly exempts Wikipedia and GitHub; the conflict is not silently resolved.
The learned gold-corpus quality classifier is intentionally rejected to limit demographic and dialect erasure, but simple heuristics can still encode bias and lose useful text.
Similarity thresholds reduce selected overlap and duplication; they do not prove absence of paraphrases, memorization, or later-benchmark leakage.

claims.statement: A seven-mixture sweep over four downstream losses informs the source weights. Separate 1.4B-model experiments using only 5GB from each candidate web corpus report that heuristic filtering and exact/fuzzy deduplication progressively improve three evaluation losses, and the final MassiveWeb variant beats the tested OpenWebText and C4 variants on those evaluations.

locator.label: Mixture and web-pipeline ablations
locator.section: A.3.1 MassiveText Subsets Weighting; A.3.2 Iterative Refinement of MassiveWeb

evidence.support: The appendix states the sweep designs and plots the selected loss comparisons.

limitations: The 5GB, 1.4B-model proxy study does not establish that every stage is universally beneficial, isolate every stage independently, or prove full-scale superiority over all C4 and OpenWebText constructions.
The mixture weights optimize four selected losses and are not a task-neutral or rights-aware optimum.

claims.statement: Gopher's tokenizer applies lossy NFKC compatibility normalization. The appendix notes that this can collapse superscripts, reduce expressivity, and alter both training and evaluation text, and recommends a lossless normalization approach for future work; one appendix occurrence transposes the acronym as NKFC.

locator.label: Tokenizer normalization failure and model-card preprocessing
locator.section: A.4 Limitations; B Gopher Model Card

evidence.support: The appendix describes the superscript failure and recommendation, while the model card confirms NFKC preprocessing.

limitations: Byte fallback provides open-vocabulary symbol coverage after normalization; it cannot recover distinctions already collapsed by NFKC.

claims.statement: Against the best Gopher-family model up to 7.1B, the 280B model has zero or no gain on 16 of 152 tasks, gains up to 25% on 57, and gains over 25% on 79. Knowledge-heavy medicine, science, technology, social-science, and humanities tasks show many large gains, while mathematics, logical reasoning, and common-sense categories benefit less and include lower 280B results on Abstract Algebra, Temporal Sequences, and High School Mathematics. The paper labels 79 of 152 as 51.2%; direct division is about 52.0%.

locator.label: Task-bucket counts, domain pattern, and negative cases

evidence.support: The canonical text prints the three buckets, describes the category pattern, and names counterexamples; arithmetic checks the printed percentage.

limitations: Relative percentage changes mix metrics with different scales and directions; the paper itself notes that bits-per-byte compresses apparent language-modeling gains relative to accuracy tasks.
The family comparison keeps token count and corpus family fixed but not compute, optimizer scale, architecture dimensions, precision, or batch size.
Selected task categories and examples do not establish a universal capability threshold or monotonic emergence law.

claims.statement: The report evaluates 152 tasks, of which 124 have selected prior language-model results; Gopher improves the chosen metric on 100 of 124. It reports 60.0 five-shot average accuracy across 57 MMLU tasks versus 43.9 for GPT-3 and 48.9 for UnifiedQA, RACE-h 71.6 versus 46.8 GPT-3 and 47.9 Megatron-Turing NLG, RACE-m 75.1 versus 58.1 GPT-3, and state of the art on 11 of 19 language-modeling datasets, while retaining much higher supervised and human RACE references.

evidence.support: The canonical task inventory, plots, tables, and prose print the task counts, comparison counts, MMLU, RACE, and language-modeling values.

locator.section: D.1 Full Results; D.2 Pile; D.3 Language Modelling

evidence.support: The appendix exposes shot counts, imported comparator scope, and mixed wins and losses behind the summary.

limitations: The 100-of-124 headline combines heterogeneous prompts, shot counts, metrics, test sets, baselines, corpora, and publication states; it is not one controlled experiment or a universal dominance rate.
Book and article gains may partly reflect MassiveText's 27% book sampling, while Gopher remains relatively worse on Ubuntu IRC, DM Mathematics, and OpenWebText in the Pile subset.
The MMLU comparison imports baseline and human estimates, and the paper's claim of more than 30% over UnifiedQA is neither 30 percentage points nor a 30% relative gain.

claims.statement: Across multiple language-model evaluations, the 417M through 7.1B points approximately follow a log-log loss trend, but the 280B Gopher point notably deviates. The authors retain two explanations—Gopher may be under-trained, or the power law may bend at this scale—and note PG-19 as an evaluation where the trend still appears to hold.

locator.label: Large-model loss-curve deviation and competing explanations

evidence.support: The appendix plots the family and explicitly states the deviation, under-training hypothesis, alternative curve-bending hypothesis, and PG-19 exception.

limitations: This is a diagnostic ambiguity under Gopher's fixed 300B-token schedule, not a fixed-compute optimum, a fitted Chinchilla allocation law, or proof of either explanation.
Task-specific loss curves do not establish the same scaling behavior for downstream accuracy, reasoning, safety, or serving cost.

claims.statement: Naively evaluating beyond the trained 2,048-token span caused an unreported sharp degradation. Clamping relative positions at 2,048 permits longer-context gains principally on articles and code, smaller gains on books, and no gain on PubMed Abstracts, but makes every token farther than 2,048 positionally indistinguishable.

evidence.support: The appendix describes the failed naive extension, clamping method, domain-specific results, and positional indistinguishability boundary.

limitations: The experiment changes evaluation context without adding Transformer-XL segment recurrence or proving unbounded memory; distances beyond the clamp share one encoding.
Section D.6 prose calls the shorter comparison window 1,000 tokens, while Figure A11 and its caption label that baseline 1,024; the record does not silently choose between them.
The magnitude of the naive degradation is not reported.

claims.statement: FEVER evaluation leaves Gopher's weights frozen but trains a multiclass logistic regression on the language model's three label probabilities and uses a fixed 15-example prompt. Scale mainly improves discrimination of SUPPORTED versus REFUTED claims; REFUTED versus NOTENOUGHINFO plateaus after roughly one billion parameters.

evidence.support: The main result reports the scale trend and separates SUPPORTED-versus-REFUTED gains from the plateauing unknown-versus-false boundary.
The appendix specifies the frozen language model, trained multiclass logistic regression, label probabilities, and fixed 15-example prompt.

limitations: This is not task-training-free fact checking: the language model is frozen, but the logistic classifier is supervised on FEVER training data.
Performance on one label boundary does not establish a deeper understanding of misinformation, a point the authors explicitly distinguish from knowing more facts.

claims.statement: On 10% of 100,000 RealToxicityPrompts with 25 continuations each, toxic-prompt continuations become more toxic with scale and plateau around 7.1B, while 25,000 unprompted samples per model remain low and do not increase with scale. Twenty-shot toxicity classification reaches about 0.76 AUC at 280B. Scale improves Winogender accuracy but leaves stereotype-conditioned gaps, yields no clear sentiment-bias trend, and does not close the perplexity gap between African-American-aligned and White-aligned tweets.

evidence.support: The canonical main text reports the prompted/unprompted trends, classification result, and nonuniform distributional-bias findings.

evidence.support: The appendix specifies sampling, Perspective API scoring, subgroup metrics, templates, raw Winogender values, and dialect comparisons.

Appendix dialogue prose elsewhere mislabels the rising conditioned Figure 5a curves as unprompted, conflicting with the explicit Section 5.1.1 distinction preserved here.
Improved classification or average Winogender accuracy does not imply fair subgroup outcomes or removal of representational and allocational harms.

claims.statement: An approximately 800-token hand-written prompt makes raw Gopher continue a dialogue format with nucleus sampling at p=.8, but the paper shows confident errors and warns that prompting does not make the model consistently reliable or factual. Fine-tuning on about 5B tokens of mined MassiveWeb dialogue produces no significant preference in 1,400 ratings: Table A31 reports fine-tuned preference 0.50±0.04 or 0.49±0.04 depending on the move selector. Canonical v2 relabels a cell-biology example from factual to mixed factuality and explains its error.

evidence.support: The main text shows the prompt-conditioned interface, selected successes and failures, and explicit reliability warning.
The appendix prints the complete prompt, sampling method, context cost, mined-data size, rater count, move-selector caveat, and preference intervals.

The 1,400 ratings use a study-specific comparison and move-selection procedure; a null preference does not establish equivalence across all dialogue distributions.
The prompt consumes about 800 of the trained 2,048-token context and its hand-authored claims about truthfulness and bias are instructions, not guarantees.

claims.statement: The paper reports that bfloat16 parameters can become stale because small optimizer updates fail to change their stored value. In a 417M-model ablation, stochastic rounding still underperforms full precision, while retaining an FP32 master parameter copy in optimizer state matches full-precision performance and preserves roughly 1.4× bfloat16 training speed.

evidence.support: The appendix defines parameter staleness, compares the precision strategies, and reports the performance and speed boundary.

limitations: The controlled experiment is at 417M parameters and is not a repeated 280B Gopher run, so its fix is not promoted as a measured large-run gain.
The surrounding prose inconsistently counts the tested configurations and misstates one plot color; the figure and caption control the comparison.

claims.statement: The embedded datasheet says MassiveText preprocessing software is unavailable and the dataset will not be distributed outside DeepMind. The model card says intended users are DeepMind researchers, Gopher will not be public, downstream use requires additional safety and fairness analysis, and the model was not trained repeatedly. It also anticipates toxic or biased output, likely personal information, predominantly English behavior, uneven dialect performance, and no intersectional-bias investigation.

evidence.support: The embedded datasheet gives collection dates, source-license notes, no preprocessing-software release, no third-party distribution, and predominantly English scope.

evidence.support: The embedded model card states the intended users, public-release decision, use restrictions, one-run status, and listed risks and omissions.

limitations: A public paper and embedded model card are not a model release, data license, preprocessing package, or experiment manifest.
The datasheet answers no to confidential information while the model card says personal information is likely present; neither provides a comprehensive privacy audit.
The GitHub component's permissive-license allowlist does not establish source-level provenance or an umbrella right to redistribute the compiled MassiveText mixture.

claims.statement: Appendix F reports Gopher training at 6.31×10^8 PFLOPs, or 6.31×10^23 FLOPs, and total listed evaluation at 4.72×10^6 PFLOPs. Its implementation-aware account includes a 33% rematerialization cost plus padding and repeated evaluation computation but is explicitly a best-effort lower bound excluding development, pre-emption, and other inefficiency. The carbon estimate uses 4,096 TPUv3 chips for 920 hours in November–December 2020, Georgia data-center PUE 1.08, October grid intensity 0.33 tCO2e/MWh, and estimated 283W per chip to obtain 380 net tCO2e.

evidence.support: The appendix prints training and evaluation PFLOPs, included and excluded work, hardware-time decomposition, and every carbon-estimate input and result.

limitations: The FLOP figure is a lower bound under the paper's practical account and differs from later nominal 6ND comparisons; it excludes research development, failed or pre-empted work, and other operational overhead.
The 380-tCO2e result is an estimate from chip power, facility efficiency, time, and a monthly grid factor rather than direct whole-project energy and emissions measurement.
Evaluation FLOPs reflect repeated common-prefix computation that the authors estimate could be reduced by 4–100× depending on the task.

claims.statement: The public Gopher artifacts inspected for this audit are the DeepMind/arXiv paper PDFs and arXiv publication-source archives. The v1 and v2 archives contain duplicated TeX, bibliography, cache fragments, and figures but no executable training/evaluation code, weights, tokenizer, prepared MassiveText data, environment lock, or run manifest. Both PDFs say all rights reserved; arXiv's non-exclusive distribution license authorizes repository distribution rather than a general reuse grant for the paper, model, code, data, or third-party material.

evidence.support: The full archive contains publication files and no executable experiment or model/data package.
The full canonical archive changes publication text/assets but still contains no experiment package or archive-level license.

evidence.support: The canonical paper states all rights reserved and explicitly says neither model nor dataset will be public.
The record-linked terms grant arXiv distribution rights rather than downstream public reuse rights.

claims.statement: PaLM is a dense causal decoder-only Transformer family. Each block uses SwiGLU, parallel attention and MLP paths, shared key/value projections across heads, RoPE, tied input/output embeddings, and no dense-kernel or layer-norm biases. claims.statement: OPT initializes weights from a zero-mean normal distribution with standard deviation .006, scales output-layer initialization by 1/√(2L), sets biases to zero, uses ReLU and 2,048-token sequences, and trains with AdamW β1=.9, β2=.95, weight decay .1, dropout .1 outside embeddings, and gradient clipping initially at 1.0. Its nominal linear schedule warms OPT-175B for 2,000 steps, warms smaller models for 375M tokens, and decays to 10% of peak learning rate over 300B tokens, with constant model-specific batches. The official completion note records 300B token exposures and 4.30×10^23 FLOPs for OPT-175B; its roughly 33-day figure assumes uninterrupted training on 1,024 A100s and is not the observed elapsed time or the paper's realized 992-GPU topology.

claims.statement: Across two months, OPT-175B hardware failures caused at least 35 manual restarts, more than 100 hosts to be cycled, and an estimated 70-plus automatic restarts. Other live interventions temporarily switched to SGD before reverting to AdamW, reset the loss scaler with mixed success, and upgraded Megatron to reduce activation pressure and improve throughput.
